are difficult for ordinary readers to notice
can be inferred from features of the translated text
choice_notes: the passage says neither approach is a failure
no preface is mentioned in the passage
"Legible" implies the opposite, that they can be read off the text
correct
items.explanation: "Legible" is used figuratively: the translator's decisions leave traces a reader can read, which is why two versions visibly differ in warmth, contrast, or rhyme.
items.skill_note: A visual metaphor in an argument usually means "detectable", not "written down".

items.passage: Migrating songbirds inherit a magnetic compass. Hand-raised birds that have never seen a migration show the same orientation as wild ones, and their bearing shifts when the ambient field is altered. Navigation, on this account, is a matter of reading a field that is always present and never clouded over.
items.passage2: Inheritance cannot be the whole story. Young birds of many species migrate in the company of adults, and birds raised without experienced companions take longer to reach their wintering grounds and make more errors. If the route were simply inherited, experience should not matter. What looks like an innate map is more likely a compass refined by imitation.
items.stem: Which choice best describes how the author of Text 2 would respond to the claim in Text 1?
choices: By denying that songbirds possess any inherited directional sense
By showing that hand-raised birds orient more accurately than wild birds
By arguing that an inherited compass does not account for the role of experienced birds in shaping routes
By proposing that magnetic fields have no influence on migration
choice_notes: Text 2 concedes a compass and adds that it is refined by imitation
Text 2 says the opposite about birds raised without companions
correct
Text 2 does not dispute the magnetic mechanism
items.explanation: Text 2 grants the compass and attacks its sufficiency, citing the difference experience makes. The correct choice captures that qualification; the denial and no-influence options overstate the disagreement, and the accuracy option reverses a detail.
items.skill_note: The response is usually a concession plus a limitation, not a flat denial.

items.passage: Bleaching is a response to heat. When water temperatures exceed a coral's tolerance for even a few days, the coral expels its algae, and the severity of the event tracks the duration and intensity of the temperature anomaly. Reducing local pollution is worthwhile for other reasons, but it will not save a reef from a warming ocean.
items.passage2: Heat is the trigger, but it is not the whole explanation. Reefs with high nutrient runoff and sediment load bleach at lower temperatures than reefs in clean water, and they recover more slowly, because the algae must recolonize through turbid water. Two reefs exposed to the same heat wave can end in very different condition.
items.stem: The author of Text 2 would most likely respond to Text 1 by
choices: arguing that bleaching is unrelated to water temperature
agreeing that heat triggers bleaching while insisting that local conditions determine its severity
claiming that nutrient runoff is the primary cause of warming
denying that reefs can recover after a bleaching event
choice_notes: Text 2 calls heat the trigger
correct
runoff is described as an aggravating condition, not a cause of warming
Text 2 discusses recovery rates rather than denying recovery
items.explanation: Text 2 accepts the thermal trigger and adds local conditions as the factor that explains variation in outcome. That is a concession plus an amendment.
items.skill_note: "X is the trigger, but not the whole explanation" is a template for partial disagreement.

items.passage: Forests may function as cooperative systems. Fungal threads link the roots of different trees, and labeled carbon applied to one tree appears in its neighbors. Older trees appear to subsidize seedlings in shade, and the network has been described as a market and as a social safety net.
items.passage2: The evidence for cooperation is thinner than its popularity suggests. Carbon does move between trees, but fungi also move carbon for their own metabolism, and roots exchange sugars with fungi locally. No experiment has shown a tree directing carbon to a particular neighbor. A network that exists is not the same as a network that shares.
items.stem: Which choice best describes the relationship between the two texts?
choices: Text 2 disputes the existence of fungal connections that Text 1 describes.
Text 1 reports experimental results that Text 2 replicates.
Text 2 accepts that carbon moves between trees but disputes the interpretation of that movement as sharing.
Text 2 argues that older trees harm seedlings by competing with them.
choice_notes: Text 2 grants that carbon moves and that fungi connect roots
Text 2 describes the evidentiary situation differently rather than repeating the work
correct
competition between old trees and seedlings is not discussed
items.explanation: The disagreement is interpretive: Text 1 reads carbon transfer as cooperation, while Text 2 lists alternatives and notes that no experiment demonstrates directed donation.
items.skill_note: Watch for pairs that agree on data and disagree on meaning.

items.passage: Life likely began at alkaline hydrothermal vents, where mineral compartments concentrate organic molecules and a natural proton gradient supplies energy. The conditions are plausible, the chemistry is plausible, and the setting explains why every living cell maintains an ion gradient across its membrane.
items.passage2: The vent hypothesis has an unaddressed problem: dilution. A vent is an open system, and molecules that assemble in one compartment are carried away by the same flow that delivered the reactants. Any account of life's origin must explain how a membrane formed and divided before there were enzymes to make one, and vent chemistry has not yet shown that.
items.stem: The author of Text 2 would most likely respond to the argument in Text 1 by
choices: rejecting the idea that early life required energy
accepting the vent setting's energy source but questioning whether it could concentrate and contain molecules
arguing that life began in shallow surface waters instead
claiming that proton gradients do not exist in living cells
choice_notes: Text 2 assumes energy was needed and raises containment instead
correct
Text 2 does not propose an alternative setting
Text 2 does not dispute the gradient observation
items.explanation: Text 2 grants the chemistry's plausibility in passing and presses a specific objection about open systems and membrane formation.
items.skill_note: A response can accept the premise and attack the sufficiency of the setting.

items.passage: Lithium iron phosphate has won the mass market. It is cheaper per kilowatt-hour, contains no cobalt or nickel, and survives thousands of cycles. For a commuter car or a grid battery, energy density is not the constraint that matters; cost per cycle is. The industry's shift is a correction, not a fad.
items.passage2: Cost per cycle explains a great deal, but not the premium segment. Long-distance trucks, aircraft, and phones are limited by mass and volume, and there lithium iron phosphate's lower voltage and heavier cathode are disqualifying. The chemistry will dominate where weight is cheap to carry, and cobalt will persist where it is not. Two markets, two answers.
items.stem: Which choice best describes how the author of Text 2 would respond to Text 1's claim that lithium iron phosphate "has won the mass market"?
choices: By denying that the chemistry has any cost advantage
By arguing that cobalt chemistry is cheaper per cycle
By accepting the claim for weight-tolerant applications while denying that it generalizes
By claiming that grid storage requires high energy density
choice_notes: Text 2 grants that cost per cycle explains a great deal
Text 2 does not dispute the cost comparison
correct
Text 2 places grid storage on the weight-tolerant side
items.explanation: Text 2 endorses the cost logic and then segments the market, saying the chemistry wins where weight is cheap to carry and loses where it is not.
items.skill_note: Segmenting a market is a way of accepting a claim locally while limiting its scope.

items.passage: Ground-based telescopes now rival space telescopes for many observations. Adaptive optics measures atmospheric distortion with a guide star and corrects it with a deformable mirror hundreds of times per second. The correction is real-time and optical, and it restores much of the resolution the atmosphere removes.
items.passage2: The mirror is only half the correction. A guide star samples a column of air, not the whole field, and the correction degrades away from it. Modern instruments increasingly rely on post-processing: taking thousands of short exposures, selecting the sharpest, and reconstructing an image computationally. Much of the improvement attributed to hardware is really statistics.
items.stem: The author of Text 2 would most likely characterize Text 1's account of adaptive optics as
choices: wrong about the existence of atmospheric distortion
accurate about the mechanism but incomplete about how image quality is achieved
choice_notes: Text 2 does not say the mechanism has changed
Text 2 begins from atmospheric distortion
correct
Text 2 explicitly says the mirror is only half the correction
items.explanation: Text 2 accepts the deformable mirror and adds computational post-processing plus the limited field of a guide star, which makes Text 1 accurate but partial.
items.skill_note: "Only half" is the signal of a partial endorsement.

items.passage: Planting trees is among the cheapest cooling measures a city can adopt. A mature canopy lowers surface temperature, cuts air-conditioning demand, and absorbs stormwater. The costs are front-loaded and the benefits accrue for decades, which makes trees an unusually good public investment.
items.passage2: Cheap to plant is not cheap to keep. A street tree needs water for its first years, pruning, and eventual removal, and in a dry climate the water can exceed the cooling benefit. Cities that count only planting costs have budgeted for a photograph. The investment is good only where maintenance is funded for the life of the tree.
items.stem: The disagreement between the two texts is best described as a difference over
choices: whether street trees provide cooling benefits
what costs should be counted in evaluating a planting program
whether stormwater absorption matters in cities
choice_notes: both accept the cooling benefit
correct
only Text 1 mentions stormwater
Text 2 raises pruning as one maintenance item, which Text 1 does not dispute
items.explanation: Text 1 counts planting costs against decades of benefits; Text 2 insists on lifetime maintenance. The dispute is about the accounting boundary.
items.skill_note: Many policy disagreements reduce to what belongs inside the cost boundary.

items.passage: The telegraph made a national market in news. A dispatch filed in one city could appear in another the same day, and papers began to carry the same wire copy. For the first time, readers in distant places encountered the same account of the same event at the same time, which is the material basis of a shared public.
items.passage2: Shared copy is not shared attention. Most readers encountered wire news secondhand, in local papers that cut it to fit and mixed it with local items, and the wire services sold different reports to different clients. The telegraph standardized the supply of news, but the reading of it remained local and uneven.
items.stem: The author of Text 2 would most likely respond to Text 1's claim about "a shared public" by
choices: arguing that standardized supply does not by itself produce a shared experience of the news
denying that wire copy reached distant cities
claiming that local papers refused to print wire copy
asserting that the telegraph had no effect on news gathering
choice_notes: correct
Text 2 accepts that wire copy circulated
Text 2 says local papers cut and mixed it, not that they refused it
Text 2 credits the telegraph with standardizing supply
items.explanation: Text 2 distinguishes the supply of identical copy from the experience of reading it, which it says stayed local. That undercuts the inference from one to the other.
items.skill_note: "X is not Y" responses attack an inference, not the underlying fact.

items.passage: The telegraph made a national market in news. A dispatch filed in one city could appear in another the same day, and papers began to carry the same wire copy. For the first time, readers in distant places encountered the same account of the same event at the same time, which is the material basis of a shared public.
items.passage2: Shared copy is not shared attention. Most readers encountered wire news secondhand, in local papers that cut it to fit and mixed it with local items, and the wire services sold different reports to different clients. The telegraph standardized the supply of news, but the reading of it remained local and uneven.
items.stem: Both texts agree that the telegraph
choices: created a single national reading public
made news travel faster and more widely than before
choice_notes: Text 2 disputes this conclusion
correct
Text 2 describes local papers as active intermediaries
accuracy is not discussed in either text
items.explanation: Text 1 emphasizes same-day transmission; Text 2 calls the telegraph a standardizer of supply, which presupposes faster, wider distribution.
items.skill_note: Agreement can rest on a premise the second text uses rather than states.

items.passage: Recording changed improvisation by making it repeatable. Once a solo could be played back, it could be studied, copied, and judged against others, and musicians began to play for the record rather than for the room. The audience for a performance became everyone who would ever hear it, and the performance became a text.
items.passage2: Repeatability did not make the music fixed. Musicians who transcribed records used them as starting points, and the practice spread ideas faster than it standardized them. The record preserved one night, but it also circulated that night to players who had never heard the band live, who then did something else with it. Fixation and proliferation were the same process.
items.stem: Which choice best captures the difference between the two texts' claims about recording?
choices: Text 1 stresses that recording fixed performances, while Text 2 stresses that fixed recordings circulated and were transformed.
Text 1 argues that recording harmed jazz, while Text 2 argues that it had no effect.
Text 1 focuses on audiences, while Text 2 focuses on record companies.
Text 1 discusses improvisation, while Text 2 discusses composition.
choice_notes: correct
Text 2 credits recording with real effects
Text 2 does not discuss record companies
both texts discuss improvisation
items.explanation: The texts share a premise about repeatability and diverge on its consequence: fixation for Text 1, circulation and transformation for Text 2.
items.skill_note: Look for the shared premise first; the difference usually sits in the consequence.

items.passage: Recording changed improvisation by making it repeatable. Once a solo could be played back, it could be studied, copied, and judged against others, and musicians began to play for the record rather than for the room. The audience for a performance became everyone who would ever hear it, and the performance became a text.
items.passage2: Repeatability did not make the music fixed. Musicians who transcribed records used them as starting points, and the practice spread ideas faster than it standardized them. The record preserved one night, but it also circulated that night to players who had never heard the band live, who then did something else with it. Fixation and proliferation were the same process.
items.stem: Both texts agree that recording
choices: made performances available to people beyond the original audience
reduced the number of people who listened to jazz
choice_notes: correct
Text 2 says musicians continued to transform what they heard
Text 2 says the practice spread ideas faster than it standardized them
both texts imply expanded audiences
items.explanation: Text 1 says the audience became everyone who would ever hear the recording; Text 2 says records reached players who never heard the band live.
items.skill_note: The agreed fact is often the one both texts use as a starting point.

items.passage: The Voting Rights Act of 1965 transformed American democracy. Within a decade, registration among Black voters in the covered states rose from a small fraction to a level approaching the national average, and the number of Black elected officials increased many times over. The law worked because it was enforced.
items.passage2: The gains were real, but the law's effectiveness depended on provisions that were temporary and contested. Registration rose where federal examiners were present and lagged where they were not; when the preclearance formula was later struck down, several states changed procedures within days. A right written on paper is not a right exercised, and the difference is administrative.
items.stem: Which choice best describes the relationship between the two texts?
choices: Text 2 accepts the gains Text 1 describes but emphasizes how dependent they were on administrative enforcement.
Text 2 denies that registration increased after 1965.
Text 1 argues that federal examiners were unnecessary.
Text 2 argues that the law had no effect on elected officials.
choice_notes: correct
Text 2 calls the gains real
Text 1 credits enforcement, so it does not dismiss examiners
Text 2 does not address elected officials
items.explanation: Text 2 begins by conceding the gains and then attributes them to provisions that could be removed, which qualifies Text 1's account without denying the outcome.
items.skill_note: Concession-then-qualification is the most common cross-text structure on the SAT.

items.passage: Coral reefs build their structure from calcium carbonate, which the polyps secrete slowly over decades. When seawater warms, the algae living inside the polyps abandon them and the coral loses its colour, a process called bleaching. [Bleached coral is not necessarily dead, but if the algae do not return within a few weeks the polyps starve and the reef begins to erode.] Some researchers now argue that the more useful measure of a reef's health is not its colour but the rate at which it is building new carbonate.
items.stem: The sentence in brackets primarily serves to
choices: qualify a possible misunderstanding by distinguishing bleaching from death while noting the real risk
provide evidence that bleaching always leads to the collapse of a reef
describe the chemical process by which polyps secrete calcium carbonate
introduce the researchers' view that colour should be the primary measure of health
choice_notes: correct
overstates: the text says the coral is 'not necessarily dead'
describes a different earlier sentence
the text argues the opposite at the end
items.explanation: The sentence corrects an assumption ('not necessarily dead') and then names the actual danger (starvation and erosion). That is a qualification, not evidence for the stronger claim in the second choice.
items.skill_note: Ask what the sentence does to the argument, not what it says.

items.passage: The paleontologist's reconstruction [cast] doubt on the assumption that the species walked upright, since the hip joint she recovered was angled like that of a knuckle-walker.
items.stem: As used in the text, what does the word "cast" most nearly mean?
choice_notes: a sense this passage rules out
a related but wrong sense
correct
another common sense of the word
items.explanation: "Cast doubt" means to direct or place doubt; the hip joint is the evidence that produces it, not a theatrical company.
items.skill_note: The trap is "a group of actors": a real sense of "cast", but nothing in this passage supports it.

items.passage: The rise in infections was [checked] only when the city closed two of its three public fountains, which had been recycling water through a filtration system that no longer met code.
items.stem: As used in the text, what does the word "checked" most nearly mean?
choices: a written order to a bank
choice_notes: a sense this passage rules out
another common sense of the word
a related but wrong sense
correct
items.explanation: Closing the fountains halted the rise, so the verb means restrained; no one was verifying anything.
items.skill_note: The trap is "to examine for accuracy": a real sense of "check", but nothing in this passage supports it.

items.passage: The masons [dressed] each limestone block with a mallet and a wide chisel before setting it, since the cathedral's facade was to be left unpainted and every joint would remain visible.
items.stem: As used in the text, what does the word "dressed" most nearly mean?
choice_notes: correct
a related but wrong sense
a sense this passage rules out
another common sense of the word
items.explanation: Mallet and chisel shape stone; the masons are finishing surfaces, not clothing themselves.
items.skill_note: The trap is "put clothes on": a real sense of "dress", but nothing in this passage supports it.

items.passage: The historian's objection is [grounded] in a misreading of the ledger: she takes the column headed "received" to record income, when in fact it records goods delivered to the warehouse.
items.stem: As used in the text, what does the word "grounded" most nearly mean?
choice_notes: another common sense of the word
a sense this passage rules out
correct
a related but wrong sense
items.explanation: The objection rests on an interpretation of the ledger, so it is based on one, not covered with dirt.
items.skill_note: The trap is "covered with soil": a real sense of "ground", but nothing in this passage supports it.

items.passage: The lower court's ruling still [holds] in three of the four districts, even though the appellate panel questioned its reasoning and invited a fresh challenge.
items.stem: As used in the text, what does the word "holds" most nearly mean?
choices: a storage space in a ship
choice_notes: a sense this passage rules out
correct
a related but wrong sense
another common sense of the word
items.explanation: A ruling that remains in force in three districts is still valid; nothing is being grasped or contained.
items.skill_note: The trap is "grasp something with the hands": a real sense of "hold", but nothing in this passage supports it.

items.passage: The nonprofit ran a deliberately [lean] operation: two paid staff, a donated office, and software chosen because the free tier was adequate. Ninety-one cents of every dollar reached its programs.
items.stem: As used in the text, what does the word "lean" most nearly mean?
choice_notes: correct
another common sense of the word
a sense this passage rules out
a related but wrong sense
items.explanation: Two staff and donated space describe an operation run with few resources, which is the "lean" sense of economy.
items.skill_note: The trap is "thin in build": a real sense of "lean", but nothing in this passage supports it.

items.passage: Reviewers praised the collection's [light] verse, noting that its rhymes about bicycle accidents and burnt toast offered a relief from the dense elegies that filled the previous volume.
items.stem: As used in the text, what does the word "light" most nearly mean?
choice_notes: a related but wrong sense
another common sense of the word
a sense this passage rules out
correct
items.explanation: Rhymes about burnt toast, contrasted with dense elegies, mark the verse as amusing rather than solemn.
items.skill_note: The trap is "illumination from a source": a real sense of "light", but nothing in this passage supports it.

items.passage: The tapestries are a [mark] of the period's prosperity: their dyes required two years of trade with the Levant, and only households with surplus capital could commission them.
items.stem: As used in the text, what does the word "mark" most nearly mean?
choices: to write a symbol on something
choice_notes: another common sense of the word
a related but wrong sense
correct
a sense this passage rules out
items.explanation: Expensive dyes commissioned by wealthy households are evidence of prosperity, so "mark" means an indicator.
items.skill_note: The trap is "a small stain or blemish": a real sense of "mark", but nothing in this passage supports it.

items.passage: Turnout is an imperfect [measure] of a campaign's strength: it reflects weather, registration rules, and how many voters were away on holiday as much as it reflects enthusiasm.
items.stem: As used in the text, what does the word "measure" most nearly mean?
choice_notes: a related but wrong sense
correct
another common sense of the word
a sense this passage rules out
items.explanation: Turnout is being used to gauge strength imperfectly, which is the "indicator" sense of "measure".
items.skill_note: The trap is "a legislative proposal": a real sense of "measure", but nothing in this passage supports it.

items.passage: The director's memo struck a [note] of caution unusual for the season: it asked staff to document every visitor and to assume that any unusual request was a rehearsal for a theft.
items.stem: As used in the text, what does the word "note" most nearly mean?
choices: a written record of a meeting
a tone or quality of expression
choice_notes: another common sense of the word
a sense this passage rules out
a related but wrong sense
correct
items.explanation: A memo striking a tone of caution is using "note" for a quality of expression, not a record or a pitch.
items.skill_note: The trap is "a written record of a meeting": a real sense of "note", but nothing in this passage supports it.

items.passage: Repairs to the seawall will cost on the [order] of two million dollars, according to an estimate that assumes no further storm damage this winter.
items.stem: As used in the text, what does the word "order" most nearly mean?
choices: a command given by an authority
choice_notes: correct
another common sense of the word
a related but wrong sense
a sense this passage rules out
items.explanation: The phrase gives a rough cost rather than an exact bid, which is the idiomatic "on the order of" sense.
items.skill_note: The trap is "a command given by an authority": a real sense of "order", but nothing in this passage supports it.

items.passage: Using a sextant and a chronometer, the mate [plotted] the ship's position every four hours and marked each fix on a chart that the captain would later compare with the log.
items.stem: As used in the text, what does the word "plotted" most nearly mean?
choice_notes: a sense this passage rules out
another common sense of the word
a related but wrong sense
correct
items.explanation: Position fixes marked on a chart are coordinates being charted, not a story or a conspiracy.
items.skill_note: The trap is "a small piece of land": a real sense of "plot", but nothing in this passage supports it.

items.passage: After two years in the capital, the young diplomat was [posted] to a consulate in Trieste, where she would spend four quiet years processing visas and writing reports that almost no one read.
items.stem: As used in the text, what does the word "posted" most nearly mean?
choice_notes: another common sense of the word
a sense this passage rules out
correct
a related but wrong sense
items.explanation: The move to a consulate is a job assignment, which is the 'stationed' sense of 'post', not a pole or an online notice.
items.skill_note: The trap is "a wooden pole set upright": a real sense of "post", but nothing in this passage supports it.

items.passage: The vaccine [primes] the immune system with a harmless fragment of the virus, so that a later exposure produces a rapid response instead of a slow one.
items.stem: As used in the text, what does the word "primes" most nearly mean?
choices: a number divisible only by itself and one
choice_notes: correct
a related but wrong sense
another common sense of the word
a sense this passage rules out
items.explanation: The harmless fragment readies the immune system for later exposure, which is the 'prepare beforehand' sense of 'prime'.
items.skill_note: The trap is "of first importance": a real sense of "prime", but nothing in this passage supports it.

items.passage: The manual devotes six pages to the [proper] handling of the centrifuge, including the order in which the lid seals must be checked and the only glove material approved for the task.
items.stem: As used in the text, what does the word "proper" most nearly mean?
choices: in the strict sense of the term
choice_notes: another common sense of the word
correct
a sense this passage rules out
a related but wrong sense
items.explanation: Ordered checks and approved materials define the accepted procedure, so 'proper' means conforming to standard.
items.skill_note: The trap is "in the strict sense of the term": a real sense of "proper", but nothing in this passage supports it.

items.passage: The [race] to map the aquifer before the wells ran dry drew hydrologists from four countries, each hoping to publish first and none willing to share raw seismic data.
items.stem: As used in the text, what does the word "race" most nearly mean?
choices: a group of people sharing ancestry
a channel of water leading to a mill
choice_notes: another common sense of the word
a sense this passage rules out
correct
a related but wrong sense
items.explanation: Four competing teams hoping to publish first describe a contest for priority, which is the figurative 'race'.
items.skill_note: The trap is "a group of people sharing ancestry": a real sense of "race", but nothing in this passage supports it.

items.passage: The [refuse] from the excavation was sifted twice, first by machine and then by hand, on the theory that sieves small enough to catch rodent teeth would also catch beads.
items.stem: As used in the text, what does the word "refuse" most nearly mean?
choice_notes: another common sense of the word
a related but wrong sense
a sense this passage rules out
correct
items.explanation: Material being sifted for beads is discarded debris, the noun sense of 'refuse', not a refusal.
items.skill_note: The trap is "to decline to do something": a real sense of "refuse", but nothing in this passage supports it.

items.passage: The donors' names are carved in low [relief] along the hospital's entrance wall, projecting barely a centimeter from the stone so that snow does not catch on the letters.
items.stem: As used in the text, what does the word "relief" most nearly mean?
choices: a raised design projecting from a flat surface
a worker replacing another on a shift
the easing of pain or anxiety
choice_notes: a related but wrong sense
correct
a sense this passage rules out
another common sense of the word
items.explanation: Carved letters projecting from stone describe sculpture in relief, not the easing of distress or financial aid.
items.skill_note: The trap is "the easing of pain or anxiety": a real sense of "relief", but nothing in this passage supports it.

items.passage: The committee asked a poet to [render] the testimony into verse, hoping that meter would make the dry account of the flood easier for schoolchildren to remember.
items.stem: As used in the text, what does the word "render" most nearly mean?
choices: to cause someone to become something
to provide a service for payment
choice_notes: correct
another common sense of the word
a sense this passage rules out
a related but wrong sense
items.explanation: Turning testimony into verse is expressing it in a new form, the 'render' sense of translation or performance.
items.skill_note: The trap is "to cause someone to become something": a real sense of "render", but nothing in this passage supports it.

items.passage: The entire argument for an earlier construction date [rests] on a single watermark, and that watermark appears on paper that may have been stored for decades before use.
items.stem: As used in the text, what does the word "rests" most nearly mean?
choice_notes: a sense this passage rules out
a related but wrong sense
another common sense of the word
correct
items.explanation: The argument's soundness depends on one watermark, so 'rests on' means relies on, not physically supported.
items.skill_note: The trap is "the remainder of a quantity": a real sense of "rest", but nothing in this passage supports it.

items.passage: The discovery [rocked] the ministry for a full week: a junior clerk had approved the export of a manuscript that the museum believed was still in its basement.
items.stem: As used in the text, what does the word "rocked" most nearly mean?
choices: to sway gently back and forth
choice_notes: a sense this passage rules out
correct
a related but wrong sense
another common sense of the word
items.explanation: A week of upheaval over an approved export is the figurative 'shock' sense, not geology or music.
items.skill_note: The trap is "stone or hard mineral matter": a real sense of "rock", but nothing in this passage supports it.

items.passage: The laboratory had a [run] of eleven failed syntheses before the twelfth attempt produced a crystal pure enough to analyze, and by then two graduate students had left.
items.stem: As used in the text, what does the word "run" most nearly mean?
choice_notes: correct
another common sense of the word
a related but wrong sense
a sense this passage rules out
items.explanation: Eleven consecutive failures form a series, the 'run' sense of a streak, not running or managing.
items.skill_note: The trap is "to move quickly on foot": a real sense of "run", but nothing in this passage supports it.

items.passage: The director's [charged] remarks left the room silent; no one had expected the meeting to turn so quickly.
items.stem: As used in the text, what does the word "charged" most nearly mean?
choice_notes: correct
a legal sense that does not fit remarks
a pricing sense
a literal electrical sense
items.explanation: The remarks silenced a room and changed the mood of a meeting, so 'charged' describes emotional intensity. The other choices are literal senses of the same word.
items.skill_note: Context clues ('left the room silent') decide which sense applies.

items.passage: The instrument's [fine] adjustments took nearly an hour, each one measured in fractions of a millimetre.
items.stem: As used in the text, what does the word "fine" most nearly mean?
choice_notes: correct
a quality judgement, not a measurement sense
the 'good enough' sense
the noun sense
items.explanation: The phrase 'measured in fractions of a millimetre' tells you 'fine' refers to small, precise adjustments rather than to quality.
items.skill_note: The words after the target often define it more precisely than the sentence's tone.

items.passage: Forests may function as cooperative systems. Fungal threads link the roots of different trees, and labeled carbon applied to one tree appears in its neighbors. Older trees appear to subsidize seedlings in shade, and the network has been described as a market and as a social safety net.
items.passage2: The evidence for cooperation is thinner than its popularity suggests. Carbon does move between trees, but fungi also move carbon for their own metabolism, and roots exchange sugars with fungi locally. No experiment has shown a tree directing carbon to a particular neighbor. A network that exists is not the same as a network that shares.
items.stem: Both texts agree that
choices: trees deliberately direct carbon to shaded seedlings
the cooperative interpretation has been experimentally confirmed
fungi consume most of the carbon that passes through the network
fungal connections exist and carbon can move between trees
choice_notes: Text 2 denies that any experiment shows directed transfer
Text 2 says the opposite
Text 2 offers this as one possibility, not a shared finding
correct
items.explanation: Text 1 reports connections and labeled-carbon movement; Text 2 says "carbon does move between trees" while questioning what the movement means.
items.skill_note: In these pairs the agreed fact is usually the physical observation, not its meaning.

items.passage: Life likely began at alkaline hydrothermal vents, where mineral compartments concentrate organic molecules and a natural proton gradient supplies energy. The conditions are plausible, the chemistry is plausible, and the setting explains why every living cell maintains an ion gradient across its membrane.
items.passage2: The vent hypothesis has an unaddressed problem: dilution. A vent is an open system, and molecules that assemble in one compartment are carried away by the same flow that delivered the reactants. Any account of life's origin must explain how a membrane formed and divided before there were enzymes to make one, and vent chemistry has not yet shown that.
items.stem: Which point would both authors accept?
choices: Vent chemistry has demonstrated how the first membranes formed and divided.
Proton gradients are irrelevant to the origin of life.
Dilution makes any origin chemistry at vents impossible.
An account of life's origin must explain how energy and containment were achieved.
choice_notes: Text 2 says vent chemistry has not shown this
Text 1 makes the gradient central, and Text 2 does not deny it
Text 2 calls it an unaddressed problem, not a disproof
correct
items.explanation: Text 1 emphasizes a natural proton gradient as an energy source and mineral compartments as containers; Text 2 insists on explaining membrane formation. Both therefore require energy and containment to be accounted for.
items.skill_note: For agreement, combine what each text treats as a requirement.

items.passage: Carnegie's library grants transformed access. Before them, most towns had subscription libraries or none; afterward, a reader could enter without paying. The requirement that towns fund operations ensured the buildings were used, and circulation rose sharply in the decades that followed.
items.passage2: Access was real but narrower than the numbers suggest. Many towns already had libraries run by women's clubs and mechanics' institutes, and a Carnegie grant often replaced such a collection rather than supplementing it, on terms that excluded the smaller holdings. The story of the grants is as much about consolidation as about expansion.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main point of disagreement between the two texts?
choices: Whether Carnegie funded any library buildings
Whether circulation rose in the decades after the grants
Whether towns were required to fund library operations
Whether the grants increased the total number of libraries or displaced existing ones
choice_notes: both texts accept that buildings were funded
Text 2 does not contest the circulation figures, only their meaning
both texts acknowledge the funding requirement
correct
items.explanation: Text 1 describes expansion from a baseline of few libraries; Text 2 says many towns already had collections and that grants sometimes replaced them. That is a dispute about whether the change was expansion or consolidation.
items.skill_note: When one text reframes a gain as a substitution, the disagreement is about the baseline.

items.passage: Eyewitness identification is unreliable enough that courts should treat it with suspicion. In laboratory studies, witnesses confidently identify innocent people, and confidence is a poor guide to accuracy. A confident witness is not a reliable witness; the correlation is weak, and jurors do not know it.
items.passage2: The claim that confidence is a poor guide holds for confidence measured at the time of an identification, but not for confidence measured immediately after a first, uncontaminated observation. Studies that track confidence from the first lineup show that it rises and falls with accuracy when the procedure is clean. The problem is the procedure, not the witness's certainty.
items.stem: Which choice best describes how the author of Text 2 would respond to the argument in Text 1?
choices: By rejecting the laboratory evidence that Text 1 cites as fabricated
By claiming that jurors understand the confidence-accuracy relationship
By arguing that eyewitness identification is generally reliable
By refining the claim, arguing that the confidence-accuracy relationship depends on when confidence is measured
choice_notes: Text 2 engages the evidence rather than dismissing it
juror understanding is Text 1's point, not Text 2's
Text 2 locates the problem in procedure, not in eyewitnesses generally
correct
items.explanation: Text 2 accepts a version of the claim and narrows it to a timing condition, which is refinement rather than rejection.
items.skill_note: A qualification about measurement timing is a refinement, not a refutation.

items.passage: Translation is a negotiation with loss. Every choice, meter for image or idiom for literal sense, gives up something the original had. The honest translator's preface is an inventory of what was surrendered, and the reader who wants the poem should learn the language.
items.passage2: Loss is only half the ledger. A translation also adds: it makes a text available to readers who would otherwise have none, and the constraints of the new language sometimes produce effects the original could not. The version is not the original, but it is a poem, and a constraint has occasionally forced an image sharper than the one it replaced.
items.stem: The author of Text 2 would most likely respond to Text 1 by
choices: denying that translation involves any loss
agreeing that translation involves loss while arguing that the ledger also includes gains
arguing that readers should not learn other languages
claiming that translations are always superior to originals
choice_notes: Text 2 says loss is only half the ledger
correct
Text 2 does not address language learning
Text 2 says the version is not the original
items.explanation: Text 2 accepts the premise of loss and adds a second column, availability and occasional gains from constraint.
items.skill_note: "Only half" again signals partial agreement with an added term.

items.passage: Translation is a negotiation with loss. Every choice, meter for image or idiom for literal sense, gives up something the original had. The honest translator's preface is an inventory of what was surrendered, and the reader who wants the poem should learn the language.
items.passage2: Loss is only half the ledger. A translation also adds: it makes a text available to readers who would otherwise have none, and the constraints of the new language sometimes produce effects the original could not. items.stem: The two texts most clearly disagree about whether
choices: poetry can be translated at all
translators must make choices between competing goals
some meaning is lost in translation
translation should be understood primarily in terms of what it loses
choice_notes: neither denies that translation happens
both texts assume such choices
both accept loss
correct
items.explanation: Text 1 frames translation as a negotiation with loss; Text 2 argues that this framing captures only half the phenomenon. Both accept that loss occurs and that choices are unavoidable.
items.skill_note: The disagreement is about framing, not about the facts both texts grant.

items.passage: A restoration should aim at the film the audience saw. Restorers have a duty to the theatrical release, and alterations such as replacing titles, regrading color, and removing grain substitute a modern taste for a historical one. The standard should be the print as it was projected in 1937.
items.passage2: No single print was "the film the audience saw." Prints differed from one another, projectors differed, and the negatives were never projected at all. A restorer who claims to reproduce the 1937 experience is choosing one print among many and calling the choice fidelity. The honest alternative is to document the choices.
items.stem: The author of Text 2's main objection to Text 1 is that Text 1
choices: underestimates the importance of theatrical release
assumes a single authoritative version exists when the sources themselves varied
choice_notes: Text 2 does not dispute the importance of release
correct
Text 2 notes that negatives were never projected, not that Text 1 refuses them
Text 1 opposes modern regrading
items.explanation: Text 1 sets a standard of the 1937 print; Text 2 says prints and projectors differed, so no such single standard exists.
items.skill_note: An objection to a standard is an objection to a presupposition.

items.passage: A restoration should aim at the film the audience saw. Restorers have a duty to the theatrical release, and alterations such as replacing titles, regrading color, and removing grain substitute a modern taste for a historical one. The standard should be the print as it was projected in 1937.
items.passage2: No single print was "the film the audience saw." Prints differed from one another, projectors differed, and the negatives were never projected at all. A restorer who claims to reproduce the 1937 experience is choosing one print among many and calling the choice fidelity. The honest alternative is to document the choices.
items.stem: Both texts agree that film restoration
choices: should reproduce the 1937 theatrical release exactly
is best achieved by regrading color to modern standards
cannot be done responsibly at all
choice_notes: Text 2 denies that this is achievable
both texts oppose modern regrading
correct
neither text rejects restoration
items.explanation: Text 1 wants choices governed by the release print; Text 2 says choices must be made and documented. Both treat restoration as a practice of selection.
items.skill_note: Shared assumptions are often the ones neither author bothers to argue for.

items.passage: Retreating glaciers are opening an archive. Ice cores preserve atmospheric gases, dust, and pollen in annual layers, and the exposure of previously covered terrain has yielded tools, arrows, and even bodies that had been frozen for millennia. Warming is, in this narrow sense, a benefit to archaeology: it is releasing evidence no one could otherwise obtain.
items.passage2: The archive is being read as it burns. Objects exposed by melting decay within years: wood desiccates and splits, leather crumbles, and ice patches that took millennia to form disappear in a summer. What is recovered is a fraction of what is exposed, and the fraction is whatever someone happened to find. The evidence is not being released; it is being destroyed more slowly than it could be studied.
items.stem: The author of Text 2 would most likely respond to Text 1's characterization of warming as "a benefit to archaeology" by
choices: agreeing that exposure is beneficial because objects can be studied
arguing that exposure destroys the evidence faster than it can be recovered
denying that any objects have been found in melting ice
claiming that ice cores are unreliable records
choice_notes: Text 2 treats exposure as loss
correct
Text 2 acknowledges that objects are exposed
ice cores are not criticized
items.explanation: Text 2's metaphor of reading an archive as it burns reframes exposure as destruction, with recovery capturing only a fraction.
items.skill_note: When a second text offers a competing metaphor, it is reframing the first text's key term.

items.passage: Widening a road rarely reduces congestion for long. New capacity attracts drivers who previously took transit or travelled at other hours, and within a few years traffic volumes rise to fill the space that was added.
items.passage2: The evidence on induced demand is strong, but it describes regional networks rather than single streets. A city that removes a lane from one street may see traffic vanish from that street without worsening congestion elsewhere, because drivers disperse across the grid.
items.stem: Based on the texts, how would the author of Text 2 most likely respond to the claim made in Text 1?
choices: By accepting that added capacity attracts traffic while limiting that conclusion to networks rather than individual streets
By rejecting the evidence on induced demand as unsound in every case
By arguing that removing a lane always worsens congestion on nearby streets
By claiming that drivers never change their routes in response to new capacity
choice_notes: correct
Text 2 calls the evidence 'strong'
Text 2 says traffic may vanish from that street
both texts assume drivers respond to capacity
items.explanation: Text 2 grants that 'the evidence on induced demand is strong' and then restricts its scope to regional networks rather than single streets. That is agreement plus a qualification.
items.skill_note: Cross-text answers usually combine agreement on one point with a limit on another.

items.passage: It is [safe] to say that the harbor was dredged at least twice before 1700, since two independent maps show channels in places that would otherwise have silted shut.
items.stem: As used in the text, what does the word "safe" most nearly mean?
choice_notes: another common sense of the word
a related but wrong sense
correct
a sense this passage rules out
items.explanation: The map evidence makes the statement reliable, so 'safe' means confidently assertable, not physically secure.
items.skill_note: The trap is "free from danger": a real sense of "safe", but nothing in this passage supports it.

items.passage: By 1200 the town had become the [seat] of the bishopric, which brought a cathedral, a court, and enough scribes to support four separate scriptoria.
items.stem: As used in the text, what does the word "seat" most nearly mean?
choices: the part of a garment one sits on
choice_notes: correct
another common sense of the word
a related but wrong sense
a sense this passage rules out
items.explanation: A cathedral and a court make the town the administrative center, which is the 'seat' sense of headquarters.
items.skill_note: The trap is "a chair designed for sitting": a real sense of "seat", but nothing in this passage supports it.

items.passage: The mill owners [secured] a loan against the coming harvest, pledging grain that had not yet been planted and, in two cases, fields that they did not fully own.
items.stem: As used in the text, what does the word "secured" most nearly mean?
choice_notes: a related but wrong sense
another common sense of the word
a sense this passage rules out
correct
items.explanation: Pledging a future harvest to get money is obtaining credit, not fastening anything or making something safe.
items.skill_note: The trap is "fastened firmly in place": a real sense of "secure", but nothing in this passage supports it.

items.passage: The first [sign] that the treatment was working came not from the blood tests but from the nurses' notes, which recorded that patients had begun asking for solid food.
items.stem: As used in the text, what does the word "sign" most nearly mean?
choices: to write one's name on a document
choice_notes: a sense this passage rules out
another common sense of the word
correct
a related but wrong sense
items.explanation: Appetite returning is evidence that the treatment works, which is the 'indication' sense of 'sign'.
items.skill_note: The trap is "a posted notice giving directions": a real sense of "sign", but nothing in this passage supports it.

items.passage: What made the expedition [singular] was not its distance but its decision to travel without a radio, a choice that left the party unheard from for eleven months.
items.stem: As used in the text, what does the word "singular" most nearly mean?
choice_notes: another common sense of the word
correct
a related but wrong sense
a sense this passage rules out
items.explanation: The unusual choice of travelling without a radio distinguishes the expedition, so 'singular' means extraordinary.
items.skill_note: The trap is "grammatically indicating one entity": a real sense of "singular", but nothing in this passage supports it.

items.passage: The company [sank] two shafts into the hillside in 1908, each barely wide enough for a ladder, and hauled the ore out in buckets by hand for the first six years.
items.stem: As used in the text, what does the word "sank" most nearly mean?
choices: to descend below the surface of water
choice_notes: correct
another common sense of the word
a related but wrong sense
a sense this passage rules out
items.explanation: Boring shafts into a hillside is digging them, not descending in water or a washbasin.
items.skill_note: The trap is "to descend below the surface of water": a real sense of "sink", but nothing in this passage supports it.

items.passage: Her later essays are notably [spare]: a typical page carries three short paragraphs, no adjectives that could be cut, and not one metaphor.
items.stem: As used in the text, what does the word "spare" most nearly mean?
choices: kept in reserve as an extra
choice_notes: a related but wrong sense
another common sense of the word
correct
a sense this passage rules out
items.explanation: Short paragraphs and no metaphors describe a restrained style, not an extra item held in reserve.
items.skill_note: The trap is "kept in reserve as an extra": a real sense of "spare", but nothing in this passage supports it.

items.passage: The court ruled that the company had violated the [spirit] of the regulation even though its actions satisfied every clause, since the rule's purpose was to protect downwind residents.
items.stem: As used in the text, what does the word "spirit" most nearly mean?
choice_notes: a sense this passage rules out
correct
another common sense of the word
a related but wrong sense
items.explanation: Contrasting the regulation's purpose with its literal clauses points to intended meaning, not a ghost or morale.
items.skill_note: The trap is "a ghost or supernatural being": a real sense of "spirit", but nothing in this passage supports it.

items.passage: Unless the appellate court intervenes, the injunction will [stand] through the end of the year, and the construction site will remain fenced and empty.
items.stem: As used in the text, what does the word "stand" most nearly mean?
choices: to be upright on the feet
choice_notes: another common sense of the word
a sense this passage rules out
a related but wrong sense
correct
items.explanation: An order that remains in force leaves the site empty, which is the 'hold valid' sense of 'stand'.
items.skill_note: The trap is "to be upright on the feet": a real sense of "stand", but nothing in this passage supports it.

items.passage: Nothing in the new rules appears to [stem] the flow of counterfeit parts into the port, according to inspectors who tested the system for six months.
items.stem: As used in the text, what does the word "stem" most nearly mean?
choices: a root word to which affixes attach
choice_notes: a related but wrong sense
correct
another common sense of the word
a sense this passage rules out
items.explanation: Inspectors testing whether the rules reduce the flow are asking about restriction, the 'stem the tide' sense.
items.skill_note: The trap is "the stalk of a plant": a real sense of "stem", but nothing in this passage supports it.

items.passage: The reservoir's surface was so [still] that the surveyors could read the graduations on the far staff gauge from a quarter mile away, without binoculars.
items.stem: As used in the text, what does the word "still" most nearly mean?
choice_notes: a related but wrong sense
another common sense of the word
correct
a sense this passage rules out
items.explanation: Reading a gauge reflected in water requires an unbroken surface, which is the 'motionless' sense.
items.skill_note: The trap is "up to this time": a real sense of "still", but nothing in this passage supports it.

items.passage: The design's [economy] came from using a single part to perform three separate jobs, which cut both cost and weight.
items.stem: As used in the text, what does the word "economy" most nearly mean?
choices: a country's system of trade and finance
the cheapest class of air travel
choice_notes: correct
the macroeconomic sense
an unrelated commercial sense
too narrow: the text is about arrangement, not price alone
items.explanation: 'Economy' here names the efficiency achieved by making one part do three jobs. That arrangement cut cost and weight, but the word describes the efficiency rather than a price reduction.
items.skill_note: When two choices are close, pick the one that matches what the sentence emphasises.

items.passage: The light had to be trimmed before dark, and Kettlewell would not let her do it alone until she could name every part of the lamp without looking. So she stood on the iron stair with the wick in her hand while he counted, and when she reached the top she found that the fog had come in below them, a gray floor where the harbor had been. The bell was already sounding. She thought, with a calm that surprised her, that the ships out there were steering by a light she could put out with two fingers, and that her father had done this every night for nineteen years without once mentioning what it weighed.
items.stem: As used in the passage, "what it weighed" most nearly refers to
choices: the physical effort of trimming the lamp each night
the length of her father's service at the light
the importance of the harbor to the town
the responsibility her father carried without complaint
choice_notes: the passage is about the meaning of the task, not its exertion
nineteen years is given as a duration, not as the burden
the harbor's importance is context, not the referent
correct
items.explanation: The clause contrasts nineteen years of nightly work with never mentioning "what it weighed," which is the burden of knowing that lives depended on the light. The metaphor is about responsibility, not physical strain or time served.
items.skill_note: Ask what the pronoun would have to refer to for the sentence's contrast to work.

items.passage: Bleaching is a response to heat. When water temperatures exceed a coral's tolerance for even a few days, the coral expels its algae, and the severity of the event tracks the duration and intensity of the temperature anomaly. Reducing local pollution is worthwhile for other reasons, but it will not save a reef from a warming ocean.
items.passage2: Heat is the trigger, but it is not the whole explanation. Reefs with high nutrient runoff and sediment load bleach at lower temperatures than reefs in clean water, and they recover more slowly, because the algae must recolonize through turbid water. Two reefs exposed to the same heat wave can end in very different condition.
items.stem: The two texts disagree about whether
choices: reducing local pollution can meaningfully affect bleaching outcomes
water temperature affects the severity of bleaching
choice_notes: correct
both accept the thermal link
both texts treat bleaching as real
Text 1 states it and Text 2 assumes it
items.explanation: Text 1 says pollution reduction "will not save a reef from a warming ocean," while Text 2 argues that nutrient and sediment loads change which reefs bleach and how fast they recover. That is the live disagreement.
items.skill_note: Disagreement questions require a point one text asserts and the other denies, not just different emphasis.

items.passage: Lithium iron phosphate has won the mass market. It is cheaper per kilowatt-hour, contains no cobalt or nickel, and survives thousands of cycles. For a commuter car or a grid battery, energy density is not the constraint that matters; cost per cycle is. The industry's shift is a correction, not a fad.
items.passage2: Cost per cycle explains a great deal, but not the premium segment. Long-distance trucks, aircraft, and phones are limited by mass and volume, and there lithium iron phosphate's lower voltage and heavier cathode are disqualifying. The chemistry will dominate where weight is cheap to carry, and cobalt will persist where it is not. Two markets, two answers.
items.stem: The two texts disagree about
choices: whether lithium iron phosphate is likely to displace cobalt chemistries across all applications
whether lithium iron phosphate is cheaper per kilowatt-hour than cobalt chemistries
whether grid storage is a viable use for lithium iron phosphate
choice_notes: correct
both accept the cost advantage
both place grid storage in the favorable category
only Text 1 raises geography, and Text 2 does not contest it
items.explanation: Text 1 describes a market-wide victory; Text 2 predicts persistence of cobalt in weight-sensitive uses. The scope of the win is the disagreement.
items.skill_note: Precision about scope is often the whole disagreement in these pairs.

items.passage: Carnegie's library grants transformed access. Before them, most towns had subscription libraries or none; afterward, a reader could enter without paying. The requirement that towns fund operations ensured the buildings were used, and circulation rose sharply in the decades that followed.
items.passage2: Access was real but narrower than the numbers suggest. Many towns already had libraries run by women's clubs and mechanics' institutes, and a Carnegie grant often replaced such a collection rather than supplementing it, on terms that excluded the smaller holdings. The story of the grants is as much about consolidation as about expansion.
items.stem: The author of Text 2 would most likely regard Text 1's claim that "circulation rose sharply" as
choices: insufficient on its own to show that readers gained libraries they did not previously have
proof that subscription libraries were unpopular
irrelevant because circulation was not recorded
choice_notes: correct
Text 2 argues the numbers are consistent with consolidation
Text 2 does not discuss popularity
Text 2 does not dispute that records exist
items.explanation: If a grant replaced an existing collection, circulation could rise at the new building without any net gain in access. Text 2 therefore treats the figure as compatible with its own account.
items.skill_note: A statistic that both sides can explain is not decisive evidence for either.

items.passage: Eyewitness identification is unreliable enough that courts should treat it with suspicion. In laboratory studies, witnesses confidently identify innocent people, and confidence is a poor guide to accuracy. A confident witness is not a reliable witness; the correlation is weak, and jurors do not know it.
items.passage2: The claim that confidence is a poor guide holds for confidence measured at the time of an identification, but not for confidence measured immediately after a first, uncontaminated observation. Studies that track confidence from the first lineup show that it rises and falls with accuracy when the procedure is clean. The problem is the procedure, not the witness's certainty.
items.stem: The two texts disagree about whether
choices: laboratory studies of eyewitness memory should be conducted
confidence can ever be a useful indicator of an identification's accuracy
innocent people are sometimes identified by witnesses
choice_notes: neither text opposes the research
correct
both accept that mistaken identifications occur
only Text 1 addresses jurors
items.explanation: Text 1 calls the correlation weak and confidence a poor guide without qualification; Text 2 says confidence tracks accuracy under clean, early measurement.
items.skill_note: "Ever" in an answer choice is a cue to check whether the other text allows any exception.

items.passage: Retreating glaciers are opening an archive. Ice cores preserve atmospheric gases, dust, and pollen in annual layers, and the exposure of previously covered terrain has yielded tools, arrows, and even bodies that had been frozen for millennia. Warming is, in this narrow sense, a benefit to archaeology: it is releasing evidence no one could otherwise obtain.
items.passage2: The archive is being read as it burns. Objects exposed by melting decay within years: wood desiccates and splits, leather crumbles, and ice patches that took millennia to form disappear in a summer. What is recovered is a fraction of what is exposed, and the fraction is whatever someone happened to find. The evidence is not being released; it is being destroyed more slowly than it could be studied.
items.stem: Which statement is supported by both texts?
choices: Objects recovered from ice are usually well preserved.
The archaeological record gains more from warming than it loses.
Ice patches are re-forming faster than they melt.
Melting ice is exposing material that had been frozen for a long time.
choice_notes: Text 2 says recovered objects decay quickly
Text 1 asserts the gain, Text 2 denies it
Text 2 says the opposite
correct
items.explanation: Both texts describe objects and ice being released by melting; they split on whether that constitutes a net benefit and on how well the material survives.
items.skill_note: Find the neutral observation the two texts interpret differently.

items.passage: The obituary was assembled almost entirely from [stock] phrases, offering the customary tributes to kindness and vision without naming a single event in the man's life.
items.stem: As used in the text, what does the word "stock" most nearly mean?
choices: a supply of goods held for sale
choice_notes: a sense this passage rules out
a related but wrong sense
another common sense of the word
correct
items.explanation: Phrases used without reference to any actual event are unoriginal, the 'stock' sense of commonplace.
items.skill_note: The trap is "shares in a company": a real sense of "stock", but nothing in this passage supports it.

items.passage: Peat bogs [store] roughly twice as much carbon per hectare as the forests that replaced them, which is why draining a bog releases more than clearing a wood.
items.stem: As used in the text, what does the word "store" most nearly mean?
choices: to supply or furnish what is needed
choice_notes: correct
a related but wrong sense
another common sense of the word
a sense this passage rules out
items.explanation: Bogs holding carbon over centuries are accumulating it, the 'store' sense of retention, not a shop.
items.skill_note: The trap is "a shop that sells goods": a real sense of "store", but nothing in this passage supports it.

items.passage: The committee [struck] the disputed sentence from the final report and replaced it with a footnote acknowledging that the evidence was inconclusive.
items.stem: As used in the text, what does the word "struck" most nearly mean?
choice_notes: another common sense of the word
a sense this passage rules out
a related but wrong sense
correct
items.explanation: Replacing a sentence with a footnote means it was removed, the editorial sense of 'strike'.
items.skill_note: The trap is "to hit repeatedly": a real sense of "strike", but nothing in this passage supports it.

items.passage: The book is a [study] in institutional failure: four chapters on the same agency, each describing a reform that was announced, funded, and never carried out.
items.stem: As used in the text, what does the word "study" most nearly mean?
choices: a careful examination of a subject
a room set aside for reading
a preliminary sketch for a painting
choice_notes: correct
a related but wrong sense
another common sense of the word
a sense this passage rules out
items.explanation: Four chapters analyzing one agency make the book an examination, the noun sense of 'study'.
items.skill_note: The trap is "a room set aside for reading": a real sense of "study", but nothing in this passage supports it.

items.passage: A [score] of nesting pairs returned to the island this spring, up from just four in 1998, when the rats were finally removed and the burrows began to hold.
items.stem: As used in the text, what does the word "score" most nearly mean?

the points earned in a game
choice_notes: a sense this passage rules out
a related but wrong sense
correct
another common sense of the word

items.passage: The judge [stayed] the order for ninety days to give the agency time to produce the documents it had withheld, a delay the plaintiffs did not oppose.
items.stem: As used in the text, what does the word "stayed" most nearly mean?
choice_notes: a related but wrong sense
correct
a sense this passage rules out
another common sense of the word

items.skill_note: The trap is "to remain in a place": a real sense of "stay", but nothing in this passage supports it.

items.passage: Adding lime raises the pH of acidic soil and makes phosphorus available to roots. ______, fields that had failed for years began to yield within two seasons.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
choice_notes: wrong relationship: Similarly
wrong relationship: For example
correct
wrong relationship: Nevertheless
items.explanation: The improved yield follows from the changed soil chemistry, so the blank marks cause and effect; 'nevertheless' would signal a reversal that never occurs.
items.skill_note: 'As a result' and 'nevertheless' both sound formal. Only one claims the second fact was caused by the first.

items.passage: Bats navigate by emitting calls and reading the returning echoes. ______, some deep-sea fish sense the electrical fields of nearby prey, relying on a sense no human possesses.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
choice_notes: wrong relationship: However
correct
wrong relationship: Consequently
wrong relationship: In short
items.explanation: Two unrelated animals are being compared as parallel cases of non-visual sensing, so the blank marks similarity.
items.skill_note: Different species and different senses, but the same underlying point: similarity survives a change of topic.

items.passage: The harbor silted up after the upstream forest was cleared for charcoal. ______, the customs house moved three miles inland, where its foundations still stand beside a wheat field.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
choice_notes: correct
wrong relationship: However
wrong relationship: For example
wrong relationship: In addition
items.explanation: The customs house relocation was caused by the silting, so the blank marks a result.
items.skill_note: Physical cause, institutional effect. 'However' is the trap for anyone reading two unrelated facts.

items.passage: The survey recorded the height of each tree and its distance from the road. ______, it noted whether the trunk showed signs of damage from vehicles.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
choice_notes: wrong relationship: By contrast
wrong relationship: For instance
wrong relationship: Thus
correct
items.explanation: A third measurement is added to two others, so the blank is additive.
items.skill_note: Three measurements from one survey are cumulative. Nothing is being contrasted or concluded.

items.passage: Marine animals with very different ancestors have converged on remarkably similar body shapes. ______, dolphins, ichthyosaurs, and tunas all arrived at a streamlined, torpedo-like form.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
choice_notes: wrong relationship: Meanwhile
correct
wrong relationship: However
wrong relationship: Therefore
items.explanation: The three animals are examples of the convergence just described, so the blank introduces an illustration.
items.skill_note: A list of species after a general claim is an example, even when the list is long.

items.passage: The lake's level fell by four meters after the irrigation canal opened in 1962. ______, the reed beds that had sheltered spawning fish dried out within a decade.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
choice_notes: correct
wrong relationship: Likewise
wrong relationship: Nevertheless
wrong relationship: For instance
items.explanation: The reed beds died because the water level dropped, so the blank marks an effect of the falling lake.
items.skill_note: The second sentence is caused by the first. 'Likewise' would make it a parallel case rather than a result.

items.passage: Some inventions arrive decades before anyone needs them. ______, a working fax machine was demonstrated in 1843, thirty-three years before the telephone was patented.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
choice_notes: wrong relationship: Meanwhile
wrong relationship: Consequently
correct
wrong relationship: However
items.explanation: The 1843 machine is a case of the general claim, so the blank introduces an example.
items.skill_note: The date is startling, but it supports the claim rather than contradicting it.

items.passage: Workers poured the foundation in March. ______, the steel frame went up in six weeks, faster than the schedule allowed.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
choice_notes: wrong relationship: For example
wrong relationship: However
wrong relationship: Therefore
correct
items.explanation: The frame went up after the foundation was poured, so the blank marks the next step in a construction sequence.
items.skill_note: Chronology: foundation, then frame. No contrast and no causation is asserted.

items.passage: The report recommends widening the sidewalk along the market frontage. ______, it urges the city to plant shade trees on the same block before the next summer.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
choice_notes: wrong relationship: However
wrong relationship: For example
wrong relationship: Consequently
correct
items.explanation: A second recommendation is added to the first, so the blank is additive.
items.skill_note: Two recommendations, same direction. 'Consequently' would claim the trees follow from the wider sidewalk.

items.passage: The printing press cut the cost of a printed page by roughly ninety percent. ______, pamphlets that had circulated in hundreds began to circulate in tens of thousands.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
choice_notes: wrong relationship: Nevertheless
correct
wrong relationship: For instance
wrong relationship: Similarly
items.explanation: The larger print runs were produced by the lower cost, so the blank marks cause and effect.
items.skill_note: Cheap pages, many copies. The second sentence is the economic consequence of the first.

items.passage: The city banned leaded gasoline in 1986. ______, average blood lead levels in children fell by more than half within five years.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
choice_notes: correct
wrong relationship: Similarly
wrong relationship: For example
wrong relationship: However
items.explanation: The decline in blood lead followed the ban, so the blank marks a result of the policy.
items.skill_note: Policy then outcome. 'Similarly' would make the decline a parallel case rather than an effect.

items.passage: The first edition sold poorly and was remaindered within two years. ______, the second, issued with a new preface and a lower price, went through four printings in a single year.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
choice_notes: wrong relationship: Therefore
wrong relationship: Likewise
correct
wrong relationship: For instance
items.explanation: The second edition's success reverses the first edition's failure, so the blank marks contrast.
items.skill_note: Same book, opposite outcomes. The later success is not caused by the earlier failure.

items.passage: The law requires inspectors to file a report within ten days of every site visit. ______, it obliges them to publish those reports on a public website within thirty.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
choice_notes: correct
wrong relationship: For instance
wrong relationship: However
wrong relationship: Therefore
items.explanation: A second obligation is added to the first, so the blank is additive.
items.skill_note: Two duties in one statute. Neither causes the other.

items.passage: The earliest telescopes used glass lenses, which had to be ground to a curve and mounted at both ends of a tube. ______, reflecting telescopes used a mirror that could be supported from behind, allowing far larger instruments.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
choice_notes: wrong relationship: In addition
wrong relationship: Therefore
correct
wrong relationship: For instance
items.explanation: Two designs are set against each other, so the blank marks contrast between them; the second does not follow from the first.
items.skill_note: Same purpose, different engineering. The comparison is oppositional, not additive.

items.passage: The volcano ejected ash into the stratosphere, where it reflected sunlight for eighteen months. ______, global temperatures fell by half a degree the following year.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
choice_notes: wrong relationship: For example
correct
wrong relationship: Nevertheless
wrong relationship: Similarly
items.explanation: The temperature drop was produced by the reflective ash, so the blank marks an effect.
items.skill_note: A physical mechanism links the two sentences. 'Nevertheless' would deny the link.

items.passage: The diet reduced systolic blood pressure by six points across the twelve-week trial. ______, it lowered LDL cholesterol by nearly twelve percent, an effect the researchers had not predicted.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
choice_notes: wrong relationship: However
wrong relationship: Therefore
wrong relationship: For instance
correct
items.explanation: A second measured benefit is added to the first, so the blank is additive.
items.skill_note: Two independent benefits, same direction. The cholesterol result is not an example of the blood-pressure result.

items.passage: Termites cultivate fungi in chambers they build from chewed wood, feeding the fungus and eating its crops in return. ______, leafcutter ants farm a different fungus, in gardens they weed and prune like farmers.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
choice_notes: wrong relationship: Consequently
wrong relationship: However
wrong relationship: In short
correct
items.explanation: Two insect lineages are compared as parallel cases of agriculture, so the blank marks similarity.
items.skill_note: Different insects, different fungi, same relationship. Similarity is the point.

items.passage: The dam trapped the sediment that had once replenished the delta each spring. ______, the delta shrank by nearly a kilometer a year, and the fishing villages at its edge moved inland twice.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
choice_notes: wrong relationship: For instance
correct
wrong relationship: Nevertheless
wrong relationship: Similarly
items.explanation: The shrinking delta follows from the trapped sediment, so the blank marks a consequence.
items.skill_note: Sediment starvation causes coastal loss. The cause is physical, not logical.
