items.passage: Permafrost is ground that stays below freezing for at least two consecutive years, and it underlies roughly a quarter of the Northern Hemisphere's land. What matters about it is not the ice but what the ice has preserved: plant and animal remains that have not fully decomposed because decomposition requires warmth and oxygen. When permafrost thaws, microbes resume work on carbon that had been locked away for millennia, releasing carbon dioxide and, in waterlogged soils, methane. The process is slow and uneven. A thawing hillside can lose its structure in a single summer as the ice that cemented it melts, while the carbon beneath it may take decades to be processed. Neither timescale is well captured by the single number that appears in most estimates.
items.stem: Which choice best describes the main idea of the passage?
choices: Thawing permafrost is primarily a problem of ground stability rather than of carbon release.
Permafrost covers a larger area than scientists previously believed.
Methane is a more important greenhouse gas than carbon dioxide.
Permafrost thaw releases stored carbon through processes that unfold on sharply different timescales.
choice_notes: the passage treats both physical collapse and carbon release as significant
the passage gives an area estimate but does not revise it
the passage mentions methane but does not rank the two gases
correct
items.explanation: The passage moves from what permafrost preserves to what thawing releases, and then to the mismatch between a fast physical collapse and a slow microbial process. The correct choice names that double timescale, which the final sentence emphasizes.
items.skill_note: When a passage closes by criticizing "the single number," the main idea is about complexity, not quantity.

items.passage: A stalagmite grows from the drip up, one thin layer of calcium carbonate at a time, and its layers preserve a record of the water that made them. The oxygen isotope ratio in each layer depends on the temperature at which the mineral formed and on the isotope ratio of the rainfall that fed the cave, which in turn reflects large-scale climate patterns. Growing a stalagmite is slow, a centimeter may take a century, but it is also durable, and a single specimen can span hundreds of thousands of years. The difficulty is interpretation. A change in isotope ratio can mean the cave got colder, the rain came from a different source, or the water took a longer path through the rock before dripping.
items.stem: It can most reasonably be inferred that a stalagmite's value as a climate record depends on
choices: its growth rate relative to other cave formations
whether the cave has ever been open to visitors
the depth of the cave in which it formed
researchers' ability to rule out alternative explanations for a change in its layers
choice_notes: growth rate is mentioned but not tied to value
visitors are not mentioned
cave depth is not discussed as a factor
correct
items.explanation: If a shift in isotope ratio can mean three different things, the record is only useful once those possibilities can be separated. That makes discriminating among explanations the condition of value.
items.skill_note: Inference follows from the obstacle the passage says stands in the way.

items.passage: For years, lithium-ion batteries used cobalt-based cathodes, which pack a lot of energy into little weight but are expensive and concentrated in a few countries. Lithium iron phosphate offered the opposite trade: cheap, abundant, chemically stable, and long-lived, with a lower voltage that made it unsuitable for phones but adequate for cars. It was also, for a long time, slow to charge and unreliable in cold weather. Manufacturers attacked those limits by shrinking the phosphate particles and coating them with carbon, which shortened the distance lithium ions travel and improved conductivity. The result is a chemistry that now dominates the market for short-range vehicles and grid storage, not because it beat cobalt on energy density, but because it stopped losing on everything else.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the passage?
choices: Lithium iron phosphate batteries are unsuitable for any vehicle use.
Cobalt-based batteries are being phased out because cobalt is chemically unstable.
Lithium iron phosphate batteries now dominate many markets because incremental engineering reduced their disadvantages, not because they store more energy.
Shrinking phosphate particles raised the voltage of lithium iron phosphate cells.
choice_notes: the passage says the chemistry is adequate for cars and dominates short-range vehicles
the passage describes cobalt cathodes as chemically effective but expensive and geographically concentrated
correct
particle size affected charging speed and conductivity, not voltage
items.explanation: The passage sets up a trade-off, describes engineering that addressed the weaker side, and concludes with a ranking that explicitly denies an energy-density victory. The correct choice matches that arc and preserves the "not because" contrast.
items.skill_note: A main idea that quotes the passage's own concession is often the right one.

items.passage: No single telescope will ever have a mirror wide enough to resolve the fine structure of a distant quasar. Interferometry takes a different route: combine light from two or more telescopes separated by a large distance and analyze the pattern of interference where the beams meet. The resolution then depends on the separation between the telescopes, not on the size of any one of them. The technique is unforgiving. The light paths must be matched to a fraction of a wavelength, which means timing the arrivals to a small fraction of a trillionth of a second, and the atmosphere above each telescope must be corrected independently. When it works, a handful of dishes scattered across a continent behaves as one instrument the size of the continent.
items.stem: Which choice best expresses the central claim of the passage?
choices: Atmospheric correction is unnecessary when telescopes are widely separated.
Interferometry requires a single mirror larger than any ever built.
Radio dishes are cheaper to build than optical mirrors of the same size.
Interferometry achieves high resolution by combining separated telescopes, at the cost of extreme technical demands.
choice_notes: the passage says each telescope's atmosphere must be corrected independently
interferometry is presented as the alternative to a huge mirror
cost is not compared
correct
items.explanation: The passage contrasts interferometry with the impossible large mirror, explains how separation sets resolution, and then details the precision required. The correct choice holds both the payoff and the cost.
items.skill_note: "The technique is unforgiving" signals the second half of the main idea.

items.passage: The telegraph did not merely speed up the delivery of news; it changed what counted as news. Before the wires, a newspaper in a port city reported shipping arrivals, prices, and letters from correspondents abroad, all of it weeks old. Afterward, a reporter could file a dispatch the same day, and editors began to organize coverage around events rather than correspondence. The change had a cost that contemporaries noticed: because the wire charged by the word, dispatches were compressed into a clipped style that readers found impersonal, and because the wire connected many papers to a single source, one account of an event could appear in dozens of papers under different mastheads.
items.stem: It can most reasonably be inferred that shared wire sources tended to
choices: increase the number of reporters each paper employed
improve the accuracy of reports by requiring verification
make newspapers more expensive to produce
reduce the diversity of accounts that readers in different cities encountered
choice_notes: the passage implies papers relied on a single source instead
verification is not mentioned
cost of production is not discussed
correct
items.explanation: If one account could run in dozens of papers, then readers across cities were more likely to meet the same version rather than independent reports.
items.skill_note: Inference questions often ask for the consequence of consolidation.

items.passage: The Mercator projection is often criticized for exaggerating the size of high-latitude countries, and the criticism is correct as far as it goes: on a Mercator map, Greenland appears comparable to Africa. But the projection was designed for navigators, not for displays of global proportion. Its defining property is that a straight line drawn on the map corresponds to a constant compass bearing at sea. A sailor who plots a course from Lisbon to the Caribbean can read the bearing off the chart and hold it, which is precisely what a sixteenth-century navigator needed. The distortion of area is the price of that property. Judging the map by how it looks on a wall is judging it by a purpose its maker did not have.
items.stem: Which choice best summarizes the passage?
choices: Sixteenth-century sailors preferred maps that showed true areas.
The Mercator projection is the most accurate map ever devised.
Greenland is roughly the same size as Africa.
The Mercator projection distorts area in exchange for a navigational property, so criticism of its proportions misjudges its purpose.
choice_notes: no preference for equal-area maps is described
the passage grants the distortion rather than claiming overall accuracy
the passage says the opposite, that the map exaggerates high-latitude size
correct
items.explanation: The passage concedes the distortion, explains the navigational property it buys, and concludes that wall-map criticism applies the wrong standard. The correct choice captures that defense without overclaiming accuracy.
items.skill_note: A defense of a criticized thing usually concedes the criticism and disputes its relevance.

items.passage: The literacy tests used to disqualify voters in parts of the United States were not, in most cases, tests of literacy. The passages a prospective voter had to interpret were drawn from state constitutions, and the registrar, who was also the person administering the test, decided whether the interpretation was correct. There was no answer key and no appeal. A voter with a university degree could fail; a voter who could barely read could pass, because the standard was not what the text said but who was judged capable of saying it. Federal examiners later documented the pattern, finding counties in which every Black applicant in a two-year period failed while every white applicant passed.
items.stem: It can most reasonably be inferred that the effectiveness of the literacy test as a barrier depended on
choices: the difficulty of the constitutional passages selected
the availability of a written answer key
the number of applicants who took the test
the discretion of the official who judged the answers
choice_notes: the passage says the standard was not the text
the passage says there was no answer key
volume is not the mechanism described
correct
items.explanation: Because there was no key and no appeal, the registrar's personal judgment determined the outcome, which is what allowed literate applicants to fail and barely literate ones to pass.
items.skill_note: Identify the variable that explains the variation the passage reports.

items.passage: Before mechanical refrigeration, the distance a perishable product could travel was set by how long it stayed cold. Beef from the American interior reached eastern markets on the hoof, and the animals lost weight the whole way. Chilled railcars changed the arithmetic in the 1870s: a carcass could be slaughtered near the range and shipped east at a temperature that kept it edible for weeks. The effect was not simply cheaper meat. It moved slaughtering and packing out of the cities and into the plains, concentrated the industry in a few firms that could afford the cars and icehouses, and made the price of beef in New York depend on the weather in Chicago.
items.stem: It can most reasonably be inferred that the concentration of the industry in a few firms was due in part to
choices: the capital required for railcars and icehouses
the superior quality of beef from the plains
the reluctance of eastern consumers to buy chilled meat
choice_notes: correct
regulation is not mentioned
quality is not compared
consumer reluctance is not described
items.explanation: The passage notes that the surviving firms were the ones that "could afford the cars and icehouses," which implies a capital barrier that smaller operators could not clear.
items.skill_note: "Could afford" is an economic explanation in miniature.

items.passage: The first transatlantic cable, laid in 1858, carried messages for about three weeks before failing. Its brief life did not prevent a celebration, and the failure that followed did not prevent a second attempt, in 1865, that also failed, or a third, in 1866, that succeeded and was followed within weeks by the recovery and repair of the 1865 cable. The technical difficulties were formidable: insulation that cracked under tension, repeaters that did not yet exist, and a signal that weakened over two thousand miles of water. But the decisive problem was theoretical. Engineers had underestimated the effect of capacitance on a long submerged conductor, and the messages they sent were slower and fainter than their instruments had led them to expect.
items.stem: Which choice best states the passage's main point?
choices: Repeaters made the first transatlantic cable possible.
The 1858 cable was a complete failure with no lasting consequences.
The transatlantic cable succeeded after repeated attempts, and its decisive obstacle was a misunderstanding of electrical behavior rather than hardware alone.
The 1866 cable succeeded because insulation had been improved.
choice_notes: the passage says repeaters did not yet exist
the passage says its brief life did not prevent a celebration or further attempts
correct
insulation is listed among the difficulties, not identified as the decisive fix
items.explanation: The passage narrates three attempts and then argues that the decisive problem was theoretical: engineers misjudged capacitance. The correct choice combines the narrative outcome with that diagnosis.
items.skill_note: "But the decisive problem was" marks the sentence the main idea must contain.

items.passage: Online resale was supposed to be a simple matter of matching unused goods with buyers, and in one respect it worked: transaction costs fell far enough that items once thrown away became worth listing. The environmental accounting turned out to be less simple. A garment sold secondhand stays in use longer, which displaces some new production, but the platform also increases the total number of garments in circulation by making it easy to buy cheaply and resell quickly. Studies of the effect have found modest net reductions in emissions, smaller than the platforms' own estimates, largely because the displaced purchase is often not a new garment but another used one.
items.stem: It can most reasonably be inferred that the environmental benefit of resale depends on
choices: how many items a platform lists in a year
whether a secondhand purchase replaces a new purchase or another used one
whether the platform charges a commission
the fiber content of the garments being sold
choice_notes: listing volume is not the mechanism described
correct
fees are not discussed
fiber content is not mentioned
items.explanation: The emissions reduction comes from displacing new production, so the benefit shrinks when the displaced purchase would have been secondhand anyway.
items.skill_note: Find the substitution the benefit depends on.

items.passage: A translator of poetry works under a constraint that is easy to state and hard to satisfy: the version must be a poem in the new language and a faithful rendering of the old one, and the two requirements pull against each other. Fidelity to meter may require a different word; fidelity to the word may break the meter. Translators resolve the conflict differently, and their choices are legible in the result: one version preserves the rhyme and alters the images, another keeps the images and abandons the rhyme. Neither is a failure. What would be a failure is a version that claims to have preserved everything, since the claim would mean the translator had stopped noticing the losses.
items.stem: Which choice best summarizes the passage?
choices: Poetry translation requires visible trade-offs, and a claim to have preserved everything is itself a kind of failure.
Poetry should not be translated because the losses are too great.
Rhyme is more important than imagery in translation.
Translators agree on a single best method for rendering meter.
choice_notes: correct
the passage says neither approach is a failure
the passage presents the two goals as competing, not ranked
the passage says translators resolve the conflict differently
items.explanation: The passage frames translation as a conflict between two legitimate demands, shows that different resolutions are defensible, and singles out only the denial of loss as a failure.
items.skill_note: The concession "neither is a failure" narrows the main idea to the final claim.

items.passage: Restoring a color film from the 1930s is not a matter of returning it to a state it once had. The dyes in early color stock faded unevenly, so a print that has aged has a color balance no audience ever saw, but neither did any audience see the camera negative, which was never projected. Restorers work from multiple sources, negatives, separations, surviving prints, and make judgments about which artifacts are damage and which are the record of a process. A restored film is therefore a reconstruction with an argument behind it, and the argument is visible: two restorations of the same title can differ in warmth, in contrast, and in what they choose to leave unretouched.
items.stem: It can most reasonably be inferred that the author would describe a "definitive" restoration as
choices: necessary before a film can be screened
achievable if the camera negative survives
the standard that most restorers now meet
unattainable, because restoration requires interpretive choices among sources
choice_notes: screening is not discussed
the negative was never projected, so it does not define the audience's view
the passage says restorations differ
correct
items.explanation: If every restoration is a reconstruction with an argument, no version can be definitive, because the choices could have been made differently.
items.skill_note: Inferences about labels often hinge on the passage's claim that a single original does not exist.

items.passage: She worked at the kitchen table after the house was quiet, the dictionary on one side and the manuscript on the other, and the sentence she could not solve was a single line in which a woman crosses a courtyard at dusk. The problem was the verb. It meant to walk without purpose, but it carried a suggestion of pleasure that the English "wander" did not, and "stroll" was too leisured, and "drift" made her sound like smoke. At two in the morning she wrote "went out into the courtyard, unhurried," and sat looking at it, aware that she had explained something the original had merely done.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the passage?
choices: The dictionary provides a precise equivalent for the verb.
A translator decides that the original sentence cannot be translated at all.
A writer is revising a novel about a woman in a courtyard.
A translator settles on a phrase that is accurate but more explicit than the original's single verb.
choice_notes: the dictionary fails her, which is why she improvises
she produces a version, though an imperfect one
the scene describes translation, not composition
correct
items.explanation: The passage follows a failed search for an equivalent and ends with a solution the translator recognizes as more explanatory than the original.
items.skill_note: The final clause carries the main idea in this kind of passage.

items.passage: She worked at the kitchen table after the house was quiet, the dictionary on one side and the manuscript on the other, and the sentence she could not solve was a single line in which a woman crosses a courtyard at dusk. The problem was the verb. It meant to walk without purpose, but it carried a suggestion of pleasure that the English "wander" did not, and "stroll" was too leisured, and "drift" made her sound like smoke. At two in the morning she wrote "went out into the courtyard, unhurried," and sat looking at it, aware that she had explained something the original had merely done.
items.stem: The final clause suggests that the translator feels her solution
choices: clarifies a quality the original conveyed implicitly
fails because it uses two words instead of one
choice_notes: she notices the difference with unease, not triumph
correct
the clause says she explained what the original merely did
the solution is more explicit, not equally ambiguous
items.explanation: "Explained something the original had merely done" contrasts explicit statement with enacted quality, which is exactly the loss she registers.
items.skill_note: Distinguish "more explicit" from "better" or "equivalent."

items.passage: Carnegie funded more than 2,500 libraries, but he rarely chose their books. The design was standardised: a small reading room, a closed stack, and a librarian's desk positioned to see the door. What varied was the collection, assembled locally by women's clubs and school boards. Historians who study these buildings now argue that the standardised architecture mattered less than the local committees, because the committees decided which town received a library at all.
items.stem: It can most reasonably be inferred that the historians mentioned in the text believe that
choices: whether a town obtained a library depended more on local organisers than on the standardised building plan
Carnegie's architects designed each library to suit the town that received it
the size of a library's collection was determined by its building's design
women's clubs and school boards preferred standardised buildings to varied ones
choice_notes: correct
contradicted by 'the design was standardised'
contradicted by 'what varied was the collection'
never claimed; their role was assembling collections
items.explanation: The historians argue the architecture 'mattered less than the local committees, because the committees decided which town received a library at all' — so local organising, not the plan, determined who got a library.
items.skill_note: Inference answers are paraphrases of a causal claim already in the text.

items.passage: A paleographer argues that the main scribe of a ninth-century gospel book, who wrote all two hundred surviving pages, was left-handed rather than right-handed.
items.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support the argument?
choices: The scribe's name appears in a colophon at the end.
The letters slant consistently to the left, the pen strokes are heaviest on the right-hand side of each minim, and smudges cluster where a left hand would rest on drying ink.
A later hand added notes in the margins of six pages.
The book was copied on calfskin of unusually high quality.
choice_notes: no bearing on the claim
correct
relevant topic, wrong variable
addresses a different comparison
items.explanation: Slant, stroke weight, and smudge placement are the physical traces a left-handed pen grip leaves.
items.skill_note: A colophon identifies the scribe but says nothing about which hand he used.

items.passage: A geneticist argues that a variant of the hemoglobin gene protects carriers against malaria rather than merely being common in malarial regions by coincidence.
items.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support the geneticist's argument?
choices: In a controlled infection study, carriers of the variant developed parasitemia at half the rate of non-carriers, and the variant's frequency rises with historical malaria prevalence across forty populations.
The variant alters the shape of red blood cells under low oxygen.
Sequencing has identified more than 200 hemoglobin variants.
The variant is more common in equatorial Africa than in northern Europe.
choice_notes: correct
relevant topic, wrong variable
no bearing on the claim
addresses a different comparison
items.explanation: A measured protective effect under controlled exposure, plus a dose-response with malaria history, establishes protection rather than coincidence.
items.skill_note: Cell shape describes a mechanism that could matter without showing any protective outcome.

items.passage: A company claims that its merger with a rival in 2019 produced large efficiency gains, pointing to a twenty percent fall in operating costs per unit between 2018 and 2022.
items.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly weaken the company's claim?
choices: The combined company closed two warehouses after the merger.
The rival had been losing market share for five years.
The merger required approval from three competition authorities.
Operating costs per unit had been falling by about five percent a year since 2013, and the decline continued at that rate after the merger with no change in slope.
choice_notes: relevant topic, wrong variable
no bearing on the claim
addresses a different comparison
correct
items.explanation: A pre-existing trend that continues unchanged leaves the merger nothing to explain.
items.skill_note: Closing warehouses shows restructuring happened, not that it caused the cost decline.

items.passage: A limnologist argues that fertilizer runoff from farms, not sewage from the town on the shore, is driving the algal blooms that now close the lake each August.
items.stem:
Bloom days for two reaches of the lake appear in the table.

Lake reach | Bloom days per summer (days)
---|---
Upstream of farms | 38
Downstream of farms | 40

Which finding, if true, would most directly weaken the argument?
choices: The lake's phosphorus concentration has risen since 1990.
Blue-green algae produce toxins that harm fish.
The upstream reach, which receives no farm runoff, recorded 38 bloom days against 40 downstream.
choice_notes: relevant topic, wrong variable
no bearing on the claim
correct
addresses a different comparison
items.explanation: Blooms of nearly the same duration where no farm runoff enters indicate that something other than fertilizer is driving them.
items.skill_note: Rising phosphorus is consistent with either source and does not separate them.

items.passage: A utility argues that its rooftop solar program reduced afternoon demand on the grid, easing the strain that peaks on hot days.
items.stem:
Rooftop installations grew from 4,000 to 61,000 between the two years.

Year | Mean 4 p.m. demand (MW)
---|---
2015 | 1000
2024 | 820

Which finding, if true, would most directly support the utility's argument?
choices: Total annual electricity sales were flat over the period.
Mean 4 p.m. demand fell from 1000 to 820  MW while the number of installations grew fifteenfold and summer temperatures were comparable.
Three commercial solar farms were built in the same years.
The program offered a 30 percent rebate on installation.
choice_notes: relevant topic, wrong variable
correct
no bearing on the claim
addresses a different comparison
items.explanation: A 180 MW fall at the peak hour, with comparable weather and a fifteenfold increase in rooftop capacity, supports the claimed effect.
items.skill_note: Flat annual sales do not show what happened at the peak hour.

items.passage: A health ministry claims that its 2015 anti-smoking campaign, which ran on television for six months, reduced adult smoking prevalence by two percentage points.
items.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly weaken the claim?
choices: The campaign included graphic warning labels and a television spot.
The ministry spent 22 million dollars on the campaign.
Prevalence had been falling by about 0.8 percentage points a year since 2005, and it continued to fall by 0.8 points a year after the campaign began.
Smoking among teenagers fell faster than among adults.
choice_notes: addresses a different comparison
relevant topic, wrong variable
correct
no bearing on the claim
items.explanation: An unchanged rate of decline across the campaign's start leaves no detectable effect for the campaign.
items.skill_note: Spending and content describe the campaign, not its impact.

items.passage: A historian argues that a corpus of Linear A tablets was written right to left, though the direction is disputed.
items.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support the argument?
choices: The script has never been deciphered.
The tablets were found in a storeroom with clay sealings.
Similar signs appear on pottery from the same period.
Repeated sign groups begin at the right edge of the tablet, the left edges are worn smooth where a hand would rest, and overlapping strokes show each sign cut before the one to its right.
choice_notes: relevant topic, wrong variable
addresses a different comparison
no bearing on the claim
correct
items.explanation: Stroke overlap is the decisive physical evidence: signs cut before the one to their right fix the direction.
items.skill_note: Lack of decipherment is irrelevant to the direction the signs were written.

items.passage: A liturgical historian argues that a twelfth-century psalter was copied for use at Durham Cathedral rather than at an abbey in the south, despite its southern-style script.
items.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support the historian's argument?
choices: The calendar of saints in the psalter includes three feasts observed only at Durham, and the litany names a local hermit whose cult never spread beyond the diocese.
The psalter's script resembles that of southern scriptoria.
The book was purchased by a collector in 1780.
The psalter contains 150 psalms and eight canticles.
choice_notes: correct
addresses a different comparison
relevant topic, wrong variable
no bearing on the claim
items.explanation: A calendar with Durham-only feasts and a purely local saint identifies the use the book was made for, whatever the script looks like.
items.skill_note: Script can travel with a scribe; the calendar has to match the institution that used the book.

items.passage: A geologist argues that a landslide on a steep slope was triggered by a magnitude 6.2 earthquake whose epicenter lay 40 kilometers away.
items.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support the argument?
choices: The landslide blocked a river for eleven days.
The region experiences several earthquakes each decade.
The slope is composed of layered shale and sandstone.
Seismograph records place the earthquake at the moment the slope failed, tree rings show the trees on the slide were killed that spring, and the slope had shown no movement in twenty years of survey.
choice_notes: relevant topic, wrong variable
addresses a different comparison
no bearing on the claim
correct
items.explanation: Exact timing, a dated kill event, and a previously stable slope tie the failure to that earthquake.
items.skill_note: Regional seismicity shows earthquakes are common, not that this one caused the slide.

items.passage: A numismatist argues that a hoard of silver coins found in a Welsh field was minted locally rather than imported from the continent.
items.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support the argument?
choices: The field had been plowed for at least a century.
Three of the coins were struck from the same die as coins in a securely provenanced local hoard, and their silver matches the trace-element signature of a nearby mine.
Coins of this type circulate widely in northern Europe.
The hoard contained 214 coins in total.
choice_notes: no bearing on the claim
correct
relevant topic, wrong variable
addresses a different comparison
items.explanation: A shared die proves a common mint, and the metal signature ties the silver to a local source.
items.skill_note: Wide circulation shows the type traveled; it does not show where these coins were struck.

items.passage: A management researcher hypothesizes that larger research teams produce less innovative work per person than smaller teams, because coordination costs grow faster than ideas.
items.stem:
Novelty was scored on a 0-10 scale by blinded reviewers.

Team size | Novelty score per author
---|---
2-4 authors | 6.1
10+ authors | 6.3

Which finding, if true, would most directly weaken the hypothesis?
choices: Large teams scored 6.3 per author against 6.1 for small teams, a difference of 0.2 in the opposite direction from the hypothesis.
Small teams published more papers in total.
Novelty scores were normally distributed within each group.
Large teams were more common in physics than in history.
choice_notes: correct
no bearing on the claim
relevant topic, wrong variable
addresses a different comparison
items.explanation: A slightly higher per-author novelty in large teams contradicts the predicted decline, however small the margin.
items.skill_note: Total output is a different measure from novelty per person.

items.passage: An astronomer argues that a comet observed in 2023 is the same object recorded in 1642, not a new comet.
items.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support the argument?
choices: Comets are known to lose material at each perihelion passage.
The 1642 comet was recorded by observers in China and Europe.
The 2023 orbit, calculated from forty observations, matches the 1642 orbit to within the historical measurement error, including the same close approach to Jupiter in both apparitions.
The 2023 comet was visible to the naked eye for six weeks.
choice_notes: no bearing on the claim
addresses a different comparison
correct
relevant topic, wrong variable
items.explanation: An orbital match, including the same planetary encounter, identifies the object rather than merely suggesting a resemblance.
items.skill_note: Visibility and historical records show the comet was seen, not that it was the same body.

items.passage: A park service argues that reintroducing wolves in 1995 restored streamside willows by reducing the elk browsing that had stripped new growth for decades.
items.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly weaken the argument?
choices: Willow cover had begun to increase in 1988, seven years before the wolves arrived, and browsing intensity measured on exclosures remained unchanged after reintroduction.
Wolves were transplanted from Canada in two winters.
Elk numbers fell by a third after the wolves returned.
Beaver activity increased along two of the monitored streams.
choice_notes: correct
relevant topic, wrong variable
addresses a different comparison
no bearing on the claim
items.explanation: Recovery that predates the wolves, with browsing unchanged, breaks the causal chain the argument requires.
items.skill_note: A falling elk count is consistent with the story but does not show willows responded.

items.passage: A glaciologist argues that a valley glacier advanced several kilometers during the nineteenth century, before the retreat that continues today.
items.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support the argument?
choices: Local records mention a poor harvest in 1832.
The valley is fed by a high-altitude snowfield.
The glacier has retreated four kilometers since 1900.
A moraine six kilometers downvalley contains logs buried by ice, radiocarbon dated to 1830-1850, and the same moraine truncates a farm wall built in 1790.
choice_notes: no bearing on the claim
relevant topic, wrong variable
addresses a different comparison
correct
items.explanation: Dated buried wood inside a moraine that cuts a 1790 wall places the advance in the nineteenth century.
items.skill_note: Twentieth-century retreat shows the glacier is shrinking now, not that it grew earlier.

items.passage: A zooarchaeologist argues that a coastal hunting camp, occupied for perhaps a century, was used during the winter months rather than in the summer fishing season.
items.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support the argument?
choices: Stone tools at the site were made from local flint.
The camp lies 400 meters from the present shoreline.

Oxygen isotope profiles in the growth layers of recovered seal teeth record a winter birth and a first-year growth pattern that ends in winter, and the site's bird bones are all of species present only in winter.
The site was excavated over three seasons.
choice_notes: relevant topic, wrong variable
addresses a different comparison
correct
no bearing on the claim
items.explanation: Tooth growth increments and winter-only bird species both fix the season of occupation.
items.skill_note: Distance to the shore reflects later coastal change, not the season of use.

items.passage: A cardiology group claims that high-dose omega-3 supplements reduce the risk of atrial fibrillation in older adults, who face rising risk of the condition.
items.stem:
Participants were randomized to high-dose omega-3 or placebo.

Group | New atrial fibrillation per 1,000 person-years
---|---
Placebo | 24
Omega-3 | 31

Which finding, if true, would most directly weaken the claim?
choices: The dose was 1.8 grams a day.
New cases were 31 per 1,000 person-years on omega-3 against 24 on placebo, a difference of 7 in the direction opposite to the claim.
Participants were followed for a median of five years.
The supplement lowered triglycerides by 20 percent.
choice_notes: no bearing on the claim
correct
relevant topic, wrong variable
addresses a different comparison
items.explanation: A higher incidence in the treated group directly contradicts a claimed reduction.
items.skill_note: Lower triglycerides is a different outcome and does not rescue the claim about rhythm.

items.passage: A climate scientist argues that the eruption of an Icelandic volcano in 1783, the largest of the millennium, cooled Europe for two years afterward.
items.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support the argument?
choices: The eruption produced lava flows that destroyed farms.
Contemporary accounts describe a dry fog across Europe that summer.
Ice cores record a sulfate layer in 1783 at four times the usual volcanic background, and tree rings from Germany and Scotland show the two coldest summers of the century in 1783 and 1784.
Iceland lost most of its livestock to fluorine poisoning.
choice_notes: relevant topic, wrong variable
addresses a different comparison
correct
no bearing on the claim
items.explanation: A dated sulfate spike matched to two years of exceptional cold links the eruption to the cooling.
items.skill_note: A dry fog is consistent with the eruption but does not measure temperature or timing.

items.passage: A pharmacologist proposes that a new compound lowers blood pressure by blocking a receptor in the kidney rather than by relaxing blood vessels directly. In mice engineered to lack that receptor, the compound has no effect on pressure.
items.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support the pharmacologist's proposal?
choices: In normal mice, the compound binds the kidney receptor at the same dose that lowers pressure, and a second compound that blocks the receptor without relaxing vessels has the same effect.
The compound lowered pressure in rats as well as mice.
The compound has a half-life of about six hours in mice.
The compound is excreted unchanged in the urine within six hours.
choice_notes: correct
relevant topic, wrong variable
no bearing on the claim
addresses a different comparison
items.explanation: Binding at the effective dose plus an independent receptor blocker reproducing the effect ties the pressure drop to that receptor specifically.
items.skill_note: A result in a second species shows generality, not mechanism.

items.passage: The idea that forest trees share resources through fungal threads has become one of ecology's most popular stories. The evidence is real but narrower than the story. In experiments, labeled carbon applied to one tree does appear in neighboring seedlings, and fungal hyphae do connect roots. What is disputed is the direction and the meaning: whether the transfer is a tree-to-tree donation, a fungus moving carbon for its own purposes, or a byproduct of roots and fungi trading locally. A recent review that re-examined the field's strongest claims found that many rested on experiments unable to distinguish among these possibilities. The network exists; the generosity attributed to it does not yet.
items.stem: The statement that "the network exists; the generosity attributed to it does not yet" most nearly suggests that
choices: the fungi are generous to trees but the trees are not generous to one another
the physical connections are documented while the altruistic interpretation remains unproven
researchers have found no evidence of carbon moving between trees
the network will eventually be shown to be an artifact of the labeling method
choice_notes: the sentence contrasts a structure with an interpretation, not two species' motives
correct
carbon movement is reported as evidence
the passage does not predict the network will dissolve
items.explanation: The parallel clauses oppose what exists (the network) to what is merely attributed (generosity), which maps onto documented connections versus an unproven motive. The other choices convert a claim about evidence into claims about fungal or tree behavior or about future findings.
items.skill_note: Read semicolon-balanced sentences as a contrast between two categories.

items.passage: The idea that forest trees share resources through fungal threads has become one of ecology's most popular stories. The evidence is real but narrower than the story. In experiments, labeled carbon applied to one tree does appear in neighboring seedlings, and fungal hyphae do connect roots. What is disputed is the direction and the meaning: whether the transfer is a tree-to-tree donation, a fungus moving carbon for its own purposes, or a byproduct of roots and fungi trading locally. A recent review that re-examined the field's strongest claims found that many rested on experiments unable to distinguish among these possibilities. The network exists; the generosity attributed to it does not yet.
items.stem: Which finding, if true, would most weaken the claim that trees deliberately transfer carbon to struggling neighbors through fungal networks?
choices: Fungal threads connect trees of the same species more often than trees of different species.
Most of the carbon moving through fungal threads was consumed by the fungus rather than deposited in neighboring trees.
Fungal networks are more extensive in old-growth forests than in recently planted stands.
Trees in the same stand often share several species of fungal partner.
choice_notes: relatedness patterns do not address whether transfer is directed
correct
this describes where networks are dense, not why carbon moves
shared partners are consistent with the claim rather than damaging to it
items.explanation: The claim requires carbon to reach the neighbor as a benefit. If the fungus absorbs the carbon for itself, the transfer is fungal nutrition rather than tree-to-tree donation, which is the alternative the passage raises. The other findings concern network distribution or partner overlap and leave the direction of benefit untouched.
items.skill_note: A weakening finding must attack the mechanism the claim depends on, not a surrounding fact.

items.passage: Permafrost is ground that stays below freezing for at least two consecutive years, and it underlies roughly a quarter of the Northern Hemisphere's land. What matters about it is not the ice but what the ice has preserved: plant and animal remains that have not fully decomposed because decomposition requires warmth and oxygen. When permafrost thaws, microbes resume work on carbon that had been locked away for millennia, releasing carbon dioxide and, in waterlogged soils, methane. The process is slow and uneven. A thawing hillside can lose its structure in a single summer as the ice that cemented it melts, while the carbon beneath it may take decades to be processed. Neither timescale is well captured by the single number that appears in most estimates.
items.stem: The passage suggests that a single number for permafrost carbon release is inadequate because
choices: physical collapse and microbial processing occur at very different rates
the amount of carbon stored in permafrost has never been measured
methane cannot be measured with current instruments
scientists disagree about whether permafrost is thawing
choice_notes: correct
storage is described as substantial and preserved, not unmeasured
no claim is made about instrumentation
thawing is treated as established
items.explanation: The two sentences before the final one contrast a hillside that fails in a summer with carbon that takes decades to be processed. One figure cannot represent both rates, which is exactly the criticism.
items.skill_note: "Neither timescale" in the last sentence points back to the two examples.

items.passage: The case for planting trees along city streets usually rests on shade, and the shade is real: a mature canopy can lower surface temperatures on a block by several degrees. But street trees are also infrastructure with a maintenance schedule, and the costs fall on the agency that plants them while the benefits, cooler air, slower traffic, higher property values, accrue to residents and landlords who did not pay. That mismatch explains a pattern that otherwise looks irrational: cities plant trees in campaigns and then lose them to neglect, because the budget for watering and pruning is a separate line item that is easier to cut than a construction project. A tree planted without a maintenance budget is a photograph, not an investment.
items.stem: It can most reasonably be inferred that the mismatch described in the passage tends to produce
choices: planting programs whose benefits erode after the initial investment
higher taxes in neighborhoods with mature trees
stronger construction budgets in city agencies
trees that grow faster than they would in rural areas
choice_notes: correct
taxes are not discussed
the passage says maintenance budgets are easier to cut
growth rates are not compared
items.explanation: Because the agency bears costs it does not recover and can cut upkeep more easily than construction, the canopy declines once the planting is finished, eroding the benefits that justified it.
items.skill_note: Follow the incentive: whoever pays and whoever benefits determines the outcome.

items.passage: A translator of poetry works under a constraint that is easy to state and hard to satisfy: the version must be a poem in the new language and a faithful rendering of the old one, and the two requirements pull against each other. Fidelity to meter may require a different word; fidelity to the word may break the meter. Translators resolve the conflict differently, and their choices are legible in the result: one version preserves the rhyme and alters the images, another keeps the images and abandons the rhyme. Neither is a failure. What would be a failure is a version that claims to have preserved everything, since the claim would mean the translator had stopped noticing the losses.
items.stem: The final sentence suggests that the author regards a claim of complete preservation as
choices: evidence that the translator is no longer attending to what was lost
the mark of an unusually skilled translator
the only honest position for a translator to take
a technical impossibility that no translator has considered
choice_notes: correct
the passage calls such a claim a failure
the passage treats the claim as self-deceiving
the claim is presented as a temptation, not an impossibility
items.explanation: The author reasons that the claim could only be made by someone who had stopped noticing losses, which makes the claim a symptom of inattention.
items.skill_note: "Since the claim would mean" introduces the author's diagnosis of the claimer.

items.passage: The claim that recording froze jazz is a strange one, given that the music was improvised and that records are the main way anyone hears it now. What the claim gets at is a distinction between a performance and a document. Before recording, a solo existed only in the room where it was played and in the memory of its hearers; a musician could play the same piece differently every night, and often did. Recording made one of those nights into a text. Later musicians learned solos from records, note for note, and transcription gave the music a repertoire of fixed statements it had not previously had. Whether that is a loss depends on whether you think a tradition is best carried in memory or in notation.
items.stem: It can most reasonably be inferred that the author's attitude toward the "frozen jazz" claim is
choices: that it is entirely correct and needs no qualification
that it identifies a real change but describes it in terms that overstate how fixed the music became
that it is baseless and should be dismissed
that it applies only to musicians who could not read music
choice_notes: the passage calls the claim strange and reframes it
correct
the passage takes the underlying change seriously rather than dismissing it
music literacy is not discussed
items.explanation: The author grants that performance became document but objects to the word "froze," since the final sentence leaves open whether the change is a loss. That is a claim about overstatement, not about falsity.
items.skill_note: Locate the sentence where the author translates the claim into something more precise.

items.passage: A historian argues that the famine of 1846 in a coastal province was caused by the failure of the potato harvest rather than by the government's decision to continue exporting grain.
items.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly weaken the historian's argument?
choices: The potato blight reached the province two weeks earlier than expected.
The government received warnings about the harvest in August.
Grain prices in the province doubled between 1845 and 1846.
Provinces that harvested the same failed crop but banned grain exports recorded a quarter of the mortality, with the difference concentrated among landless laborers.
choice_notes: addresses a different comparison
relevant topic, wrong variable
no bearing on the claim
correct
items.explanation: If banning exports sharply reduced mortality under the same harvest failure, export policy was a cause the historian's account omits.
items.skill_note: Price movements are consistent with either explanation and do not discriminate between them.

items.passage: A linguist argues that the ancestors of a language family domesticated horses, because the reconstructed proto-language has a word for wheel and for harness that is shared across all its branches.
items.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support the linguist's argument?
choices: The word for horse differs sharply among the branches.

The reconstructed words refer to spoke-wheeled vehicles and to a horse collar, and the earliest physical examples of both appear in the region the linguist identifies, dated to the period of the proposed expansion.
Several branches borrowed metalworking terms from unrelated neighbors.
The family includes twelve modern languages spoken across two continents.
choice_notes: no bearing on the claim
correct
relevant topic, wrong variable
addresses a different comparison
items.explanation: Specific referents plus matching archaeological dates tie the vocabulary to the technology and the place, which is what the argument needs.
items.skill_note: Geographic spread shows the family expanded; it does not show what its speakers did.

items.passage: A trial reports that a new talking therapy halves relapse rates in depression compared with usual care, and concludes that the therapy's specific techniques are responsible.
items.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly weaken that conclusion?
choices: Relapse was assessed by interviewers unaware of group assignment.
The therapy was delivered by clinicians with an average of nine years' experience.
Participants in the therapy arm attended 78 percent of sessions.
The comparison group received far fewer clinical contact hours, and a second arm given the same number of hours of nonspecific support had relapse rates identical to the therapy arm.
choice_notes: relevant topic, wrong variable
addresses a different comparison
no bearing on the claim
correct
items.explanation: If equal contact hours without the techniques produce the same result, the benefit comes from attention, not from the specific techniques.
items.skill_note: Blinded assessment and attendance improve the study's quality without addressing what caused the benefit.

items.passage: A museum replaced the fluorescent bulbs in its textile gallery with LEDs, expecting the rate at which dyed fabrics fade to fall by half. After two years, the curators reported that the fading rate was unchanged.
items.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly explain the failure rather than the expectation?
choices: The gallery's temperature is held constant at 20 degrees.
The new fixtures emit almost no ultraviolet light, but the fading is driven by visible blue light, which the LEDs produce at nearly the same intensity as the old bulbs.
The LEDs were more expensive to purchase than the fluorescents they replaced.
Visitors spend an average of nine minutes in the gallery.
choice_notes: relevant topic, wrong variable
correct
addresses a different comparison
no bearing on the claim
items.explanation: Fading driven by blue light, which the new fixtures did not reduce, accounts for the unchanged rate without contradicting the physics.
items.skill_note: Cost and temperature are irrelevant to why the fading rate stayed the same.

items.passage: A forest pathologist argues that a bark beetle is killing stands of pine not by girdling the trees but by carrying a fungus that blocks their water-conducting tissue.
items.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support the pathologist's argument?
choices: Trees injected with a fungicide before beetles were introduced survived at four times the rate of untreated trees, though both groups were attacked equally, and the fungus was recovered from the sapwood of every dead tree.
Beetle populations increase in years following mild winters.
Several species of pine are affected across the region.
Dead trees show galleries carved beneath the bark.
choice_notes: correct
addresses a different comparison
no bearing on the claim
relevant topic, wrong variable
items.explanation: Fungicide protection with equal beetle attack isolates the fungus, rather than the physical wounding, as the lethal agent.
items.skill_note: Galleries prove the beetles were present; they do not show what killed the trees.

items.passage: A conservator argues that the blue in a wall painting is Egyptian blue rather than a modern synthetic pigment, despite the painting's having been restored in 1932.
items.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support the conservator's argument?
choices: A restorer's notebook from 1932 mentions repairing the sky.
The blue appears in the sky, the drapery, and the border.
The blue grains contain cuprorivaite crystals with a calcium-to-copper ratio matching Egyptian blue made before 1000 CE, and no grains show the spherical shape produced by modern milling.
The painting was cleaned twice in the twentieth century.
choice_notes: no bearing on the claim
relevant topic, wrong variable
correct
addresses a different comparison
items.explanation: Crystal chemistry and grain shape identify the pigment's manufacture, which is what distinguishes an ancient from a modern blue.
items.skill_note: Restoration records show the area was touched, not what pigment was used.

items.passage: A volcanologist argues that a massive eruption in 1600 BCE, not one in 1500 BCE, produced the ash layer found across the eastern Mediterranean.
items.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support the argument?
choices: Ice cores from Greenland contain a sulfate spike somewhere in that century.
The ash layer sits directly beneath a tree-ring frost marker dated to 1598 BCE, and radiocarbon dates on olive branches buried by the eruption cluster between 1610 and 1590 BCE.
Ash from the eruption has been found in Egypt and Turkey.
The eruption was one of the largest of the Holocene.
choice_notes: no bearing on the claim
correct
relevant topic, wrong variable
addresses a different comparison
items.explanation: A frost marker immediately above the ash plus a tight radiocarbon range places the eruption within a decade of 1600 BCE.
items.skill_note: A sulfate spike 'somewhere in that century' cannot separate 1600 from 1500.

items.passage: A trial reports that a new drug reduced mortality in patients with severe infections, and the authors recommend it as standard care.
items.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly weaken the recommendation?
choices: The drug was administered intravenously for seven days.
The trial took place in eleven hospitals across three countries.
Patients in both arms received the same supportive care.
The trial stopped after 120 of a planned 600 patients, the mortality difference was two percentage points, and twice as many treated patients withdrew because of kidney injury.
choice_notes: addresses a different comparison
relevant topic, wrong variable
no bearing on the claim
correct
items.explanation: A small difference in a truncated trial, with more harm-driven withdrawals, is too fragile to support a standard-of-care recommendation.
items.skill_note: Multinational recruitment improves generalizability; it does not repair a stopped trial with a tiny effect.

items.passage: A conservator argues that a blue pigment on a Roman wall in Pompeii was applied in antiquity and is not a later repaint.
items.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support the argument?
choices: The pigment particles are embedded in cracks that formed when the plaster cured in antiquity, and a fragment of the same plaster overlaying the blue carries a dateable mortar from the original construction.
Roman painters are known to have used several blue minerals.
The wall was exposed by excavation in 1876.
The blue matches pigments used elsewhere in the same room.
choice_notes: correct
no bearing on the claim
relevant topic, wrong variable
addresses a different comparison
items.explanation: Pigment inside ancient curing cracks can only have been there before those cracks formed, which rules out repainting.
items.skill_note: A match to nearby pigment shows consistency, not priority in time.

items.passage: The Mercator projection is often criticized for exaggerating the size of high-latitude countries, and the criticism is correct as far as it goes: on a Mercator map, Greenland appears comparable to Africa. But the projection was designed for navigators, not for displays of global proportion. Its defining property is that a straight line drawn on the map corresponds to a constant compass bearing at sea. A sailor who plots a course from Lisbon to the Caribbean can read the bearing off the chart and hold it, which is precisely what a sixteenth-century navigator needed. The distortion of area is the price of that property. Judging the map by how it looks on a wall is judging it by a purpose its maker did not have.
items.stem: It can most reasonably be inferred that the author would regard a map that preserves area but distorts compass bearings as
choices: well suited to some purposes but not to the navigational task Mercator served
superior to the Mercator projection in every respect
choice_notes: the passage's argument implies purpose-relative judgment, not absolute uselessness
correct
the author's logic cuts both ways, since every projection trades one property for another
such projections exist and are implied by the passage
items.explanation: The author's principle is that a map should be judged by the purpose it was made for. Applied consistently, an equal-area map is good for showing proportion and poor for holding a bearing, which is exactly the credited choice.
items.skill_note: Apply the author's stated principle to a new case rather than to the author's preferred object.

items.passage: The claim that recording froze jazz is a strange one, given that the music was improvised and that records are the main way anyone hears it now. What the claim gets at is a distinction between a performance and a document. Before recording, a solo existed only in the room where it was played and in the memory of its hearers; a musician could play the same piece differently every night, and often did. Recording made one of those nights into a text. Later musicians learned solos from records, note for note, and transcription gave the music a repertoire of fixed statements it had not previously had. Whether that is a loss depends on whether you think a tradition is best carried in memory or in notation.
items.stem: Which choice best describes the main idea of the passage?
choices: Transcription is a marginal practice with little influence on jazz.
Recording destroyed jazz by making improvisation impossible.
Recording turned performances into fixed texts, a change whose value depends on how one thinks a tradition should be carried.
Jazz musicians before recording played the same solos every night.
choice_notes: the passage credits transcription with giving the music fixed statements
the passage says the claim is "strange" and reframes rather than endorses it
correct
the passage says musicians often played pieces differently
items.explanation: The passage moves from skepticism about the frozen-jazz claim to a narrower distinction between performance and document, and it closes by making the verdict depend on a view about tradition. The correct choice preserves that neutrality.
items.skill_note: When a passage ends by relativizing a judgment, the main idea must not take a side.

items.passage: A district reports that schools adopting a new reading program saw comprehension scores rise by eight points in one year, and concludes the program works.
items.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly weaken that conclusion?
choices: Teachers received coaching visits every two weeks.
The district spent 1.1 million dollars on materials.
The schools that adopted the program were selected because their scores had been falling unusually fast, and scores in those schools rebounded to their previous level rather than exceeding it.
The program required ninety minutes of daily instruction.
choice_notes: relevant topic, wrong variable
no bearing on the claim
correct
addresses a different comparison
items.explanation: Regression from an unusually low baseline explains the gain without any effect of the program.
items.skill_note: Coaching and time on task show fidelity of implementation, not effect.

items.passage: A trial reports that a new vaccine reduced symptomatic infections by 70 percent, and the authors suggest it will substantially reduce transmission in the community.
items.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly weaken that suggestion?
choices: The trial enrolled 28,000 participants across four countries.
Viral loads in the noses of vaccinated participants who nevertheless became infected were as high as those in unvaccinated participants, and those participants reported mild or no symptoms.
The vaccine was given in two doses three weeks apart.
Protection against severe disease was over 90 percent.
choice_notes: no bearing on the claim
correct
addresses a different comparison
relevant topic, wrong variable
items.explanation: Equal viral loads among vaccinated cases imply they can still transmit, which undercuts a community-level effect.
items.skill_note: Protection against severe disease is compatible with continued transmission and does not weaken the suggestion.

items.passage: A consumer group claims that a supermarket merger in 2018, which combined two chains with overlapping stores in six cities, lowered prices for shoppers.
items.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly weaken the claim?
choices: Prices fell across the whole region over the same years as wholesale food costs dropped, and stores in areas where the merger reduced competition by more than half fell less than the regional average.
The merger was reviewed by a national regulator.
The two chains had overlapped in six cities.
The merged chain closed twelve stores in rural areas.
choice_notes: correct
no bearing on the claim
relevant topic, wrong variable
addresses a different comparison
items.explanation: A regional cost decline plus smaller declines where competition was reduced indicates the merger did not lower prices.
items.skill_note: Store closures show consolidation happened, not what it did to prices.

items.passage: A linguist argues that a set of words entered an island language from Latin through a neighboring trading language rather than directly from Latin.
items.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support the argument?
choices: Latin was the administrative language of the nearest province.
The words all relate to commerce and shipping.
The island was visited by Roman ships in the first century.
The words show sound changes characteristic of the trading language but absent from Latin, and include a suffix that Latin did not possess but the trading language did.
choice_notes: no bearing on the claim
relevant topic, wrong variable
addresses a different comparison
correct
items.explanation: Sound changes and morphology that match the intermediary, not the source, identify the route of borrowing.
items.skill_note: Commerce vocabulary fits the meaning but not the pathway.

items.passage: A city claims that its 2019 housing-first policy, which gave apartments and case management to several hundred people, reduced street homelessness by 40 percent in two years.
items.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly weaken the claim?
choices: Two neighboring cities adopted similar policies in 2020.
The policy provided 900 apartments with case management.

The city changed its street count in 2019 from a single-night census to a week-long average that counts people in shelters as housed, and the 2018 figure was revised upward by a third before the comparison was published.
The city's shelter capacity grew by 300 beds.
choice_notes: relevant topic, wrong variable
addresses a different comparison
correct
no bearing on the claim
items.explanation: A changed counting method and a revised baseline mean the 40 percent drop may be an artifact of measurement.
items.skill_note: New apartments show the policy was implemented, not that homelessness fell.

items.rule: A semicolon joins two closely related independent clauses; a comma alone would be a splice, no mark at all would be a fused sentence, and a colon would promise a list or an explanation that does not follow.
items.passage: Nothing in the office is locked, and nothing has ever been lost. The earliest chart in the drawer is dated 1893 ______
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
choices: ; the most recent was completed last spring.
: the most recent was completed last spring.
, the most recent was completed last spring.
the most recent was completed last spring.
choice_notes: correct
uses a colon although the second clause neither explains nor lists the first
puts only a comma between two independent clauses, which is a comma splice
leaves the two independent clauses with no mark between them, which is a fused sentence
items.explanation: A semicolon joins two closely related independent clauses; a comma alone would be a splice, no mark at all would be a fused sentence, and a colon would promise a list or an explanation that does not follow. Choice B uses a colon although the second clause neither explains nor lists the first. Choice C puts only a comma between two independent clauses, which is a comma splice. Choice D leaves the two independent clauses with no mark between them, which is a fused sentence.
items.skill_note: Both sides of the blank are complete sentences; the trap is treating the second one as an afterthought and reaching for a comma.
